💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Fall is peak season for those who want to gather last-minute information on deer and other game animals ahead of hunting seasons.
  • The advantage of having a modern trail camera is the ability to capture the action you’d otherwise miss, whether it’s an elusive buck passing by your stand in the night or the raccoon creating backyard mayhem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Fall is peak season for those who want to gather last-minute information on deer and other game animals ahead of hunting seasons. Even if you’re not heading into the woods to hunt, it’s one of the most interesting times of year for observing wild animals. Whitetail deer, elk, bears, and other animals are becoming much more active due to seasonal mating periods while waterfowl and other birds migrate for the winter.

The advantage of having a modern trail camera is the ability to capture the action you’d otherwise miss, whether it’s an elusive buck passing by your stand in the night or the raccoon creating backyard mayhem. If you’re considering a trail camera that uses a cellular network to send photos and videos directly to your smartphone, the good news is these have gotten even easier to use.

Sources indicate that while the trail cam experience improves every year, the cost of many units is more than $100, and cellular models require recurring data proposal charges, making it trickier to assess value. Images from game cameras are better than ever, even in budget models, and apps add software features often.

Sorting out what matters most to you and how you plan to use your trail cameras can be a challenge, so we explain what to look for along with sharing our top recommendations selected from year-round testing of dozens of cameras evaluated side-by-side.

The Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0 replaces the Reveal Pro 3.0 camera, our previous pick for Best Overall. Released this summer, the Pro 4.0 version keeps what made the 3.0 great and improves on it in two key areas: image quality and battery life. Reveal has one of the best apps in the space, with tons of settings and features to tweak your setup and manage your cameras and images. Updates to these basics are big usability improvements that demanding trail camera owners will notice.

It has been revealed that cameras going dead in the field is a major gripe for customers of these gadgets. You have to physically go and replace batteries, which adds hassle and cost to your experience. I tend to place cameras in early summer and let them run for several months until my hunting season starts. The problem is that active cameras can run through eight to 12 AA batteries in a month depending on the model and your camera settings.

Tactacam has tackled this issue in a few ways with the Pro 4.0 release. The brand told me it audited everything about camera operation that drained the battery and then made small tweaks to reduce power demands anywhere it could.

Tactacam has also developed sold separately R5 and R10 lithium battery packs that replace previous battery add-ons, which have the notable benefit of swapping into the same form factor as the AA battery tray, so they don’t add bulk to the camera.

Image quality in the Reveal cameras has always been solid, but the tech giant took a unique approach to dealing with the challenge of getting both crisp day and night images by installing separate sensors for each. Photographers know that night images require different gear and settings than daylight shooting, so the split makes sense. The early returns from a month of testing confirm that the quality of both day and night is much improved.

The rest of this flagship Reveal camera is impressive, carrying over from the Pro 3.0 and now-discontinued Ultra camera. The Reveal lineup now has just two similar cameras: the Pro 4.0 and the X 4.0. The Reveal X 4.0 is basically the Pro 4.0 without a built-in display screen, which saves $30 and is a great option if you don’t value the screen for aiming and reviewing images at the device.

In a recent development, as mentioned, the robust app gives you remote control over everything including photo and video capture settings, transmission frequency, night image flash, trigger delays, and more. You’re also able to launch a live stream to follow up on interesting images, but there’s an additional subscription cost and it will drain the battery quickly. There’s also built-in GPS that highlights the location of your camera on a map within the app—essential if you’ve forgotten where you placed it or if it’s stolen.

Full Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0 Review.

Industry observers note that cell-connected trail cameras are handy, but if you’re low on funds or trying to run a multitude of cameras, paying $150 and up per camera gets pricey fast. Spypoint’s Flex M2 trail camera keeps both the upfront purchase cost and recurring subscription fees reasonable. Spypoint even has a free data proposal that gives you 100 images per month if you want to avoid subscription fees altogether. (The Flex M2 doesn’t have onboard memory, nor does it ship with an SD card, so you’ll have to spend at least another $20 per camera for a high-speed SD card.).

Despite the low price, the camera’s 32-megapixel photos and 1080p video are clear and well-exposed. The Flex M2 displays lower-resolution images in the app but you can request full-resolution images when you want more detail. This is beneficial because it keeps data demands low and highlights up in the battery usage as well. After a month in the field, the eight AA batteries I was using displayed in the app at “High” strength.

Additionally, I appreciated that this camera is compact since I’m usually hauling my cameras several miles into the backcountry in a pack. If you want to run this camera year-round, I’d consider picking up the $60 five-watt solar panel add-on, which has a built-in battery and should allow you to leave the Flex M2 up indefinitely.

Industry observers note that I was impressed with the overall experience with the Flex M2, but the highlight here is the cost to purchase and run this camera. Yes, you’ll need to pay up for video or a higher quota of images, but this is a great option if you want the excitement of getting trail camera images on your phone without the annoyance of yet another recurring subscription fee on your credit card.

According to recent reports, there are two significant recurring costs with a cellular trail camera: the data strategy and batteries. Connected cameras can chew through batteries, which can add up, especially since you’ll want to use more expensive lithium batteries if you can. Sehmua’s 4G Solar Trail Camera comes with rechargeable batteries and a solar panel, which allows the camera to run indefinitely given adequate sun exposure.

According to recent reports, the camera itself has a fast trigger and 2K photo and video that can be saved to an SD card, or to cloud storage for an additional cost. The app, which is a little clunky and can be confusing due to some quirky menus and word choices, works with images that show up quickly and reliably.

Notably, even though this is a 4G cellular-connected camera, you can still use the camera to record to the SD card if you decide not to pay for one of the data aims. This is another sneaky way this camera provides solid value for its low price point.

Full Sehmua Trail Camera Review.

It has been revealed that the best way to cut down on battery costs for your trail cameras is running solar panels. While many cameras have the option to run on solar, it’s often an additional upfront cost. The new 2026 Moultrie Edge 4 Solar trail camera has it all smartly packaged together in an integrated unit that costs less than some standalone cameras.

Sources indicate that setting up solar often requires separate mounting as well as hauling out lots of separate pieces and cables to be connected. The Edge 4 Solar just straps to a tree as a single unit, ready to run indefinitely. The camera comes with a rechargeable lithium-ion battery powered by the panel, which enables you to place a camera and leave it running as long as you need. Having the solar panel integrated is convenient and compact, but you’ll need to choose spots wisely to ensure both good captures and sun exposure.

In a recent development, beyond the solar power setup, the Edge 4 is a solid trail camera with crisp 40-megapixel photos and 1080p video. The app is polished and makes setup and use hassle-free even if you’re not particularly tech-savvy. The subscription plans are in line with the industry average, ranging from $8.99 to $22.99. The lowest-tier strategy offers more than most other companies’ $5 plans (1,000 images and 10 videos) and the most expensive plan offers unlimited images and 50 videos and discounts steeply to $7.99 per month for each additional camera.

The convenience of cell-connected trail cameras is undeniable, but if you’re burned out on subscription charges and don’t mind checking your cameras manually, you can save a significant amount on your trail camera setup. The WOSPORTS Trail Camera is a budget option with impressive image quality and low one-time cost. The camera doesn’t ship with the required eight AA batteries, but it does come with an SD card.

In a recent development, this compact G600 records imagery to an SD card and lasts longer since it doesn’t use batteries communicating over cellular networks. You’ll have to walk into your hunting zone to swap cards, but the purchase price is a fraction of the lifetime cost of buying and operating a modern cell-connected setup.

Sources indicate that the 56-megapixel images and 4K video aren’t Planet Earth–level quality, but I was still more than satisfied with the pictures and videos I got. I don’t put too much stock in megapixel numbers as a true measure of trail camera image quality because these numbers are mostly inflated with software enhancements. That remarked, the images and videos from the WOSPORTS camera were sharp enough for clear identification of details.

It has been revealed that the Defend by Reveal 360 is not your traditional trail camera—it’s closer to a home security camera that’s designed to work anywhere. Ring and other doorbell cameras usually rely on WiFi for connectivity, which makes them impractical more than about 50 yards from your router. The Defend 360 uses cellular networks instead so you can place this camera anywhere with a decent cell signal.

In the field, the Defend 360’s biggest advantage is motion. Most trail cams are fixed in place, but this one adds remote pan-and-tilt control, allowing you to reposition the camera from your phone. Its 355-degree pan and 75-degree tilt effectively eliminate blind spots when combined with the wide-angle lens.

According to recent reports, like a regular trail camera, motion detection triggers photos only to conserve battery and data. A 1080p live view can be activated on demand when you need a closer live look. That approach makes sense for remote monitoring, though it feels different if you’re used to continuous video feeds from home security cameras.

Industry observers note that A rechargeable battery and included solar panel allow for long-term deployment with minimal maintenance. Setup is straightforward via the app, and the camera automatically connects to the strongest available carrier via eSIM.

In a recent development, there are a few downsides. Night footage is serviceable but not amazing, and like most cellular cameras, it requires a subscription strategy to unlock full functionality. Still, if your goal is reliable, wide-area monitoring in remote locations, the Defend 360 delivers better coverage and control than standard trail cameras.

A lifetime warranty usually isn’t reason enough alone to buy a product, but in the world of electronics generally and with trail cameras specifically, it’s unheard of and fairly compelling.

According to recent reports, with Yellowstone.ai’s Y2 Camera and Solar Bundle, your upfront cost is on the higher side at $250, but the solar panel and rechargeable battery mean no recurring battery costs. You’ll also save on gas and time, since this is a cell-connected camera, and there’s no need to visit the camera unless you want to move it.

Compared to the big-name trail camera apps, the app is not quite as polished, but over several months of testing, I did not experience any of the quirks and bugs I’ve experienced with some trail cam apps from overseas companies (Yellowstone.ai is U.S.-based).

It has been revealed that the image and video quality isn’t quite as sharp as the top tier of the cameras I’ve tested like the Reveal Pro 4.0 or Moultrie Edge 4 Solar, but it’s by no means unacceptable. I was impressed by features such as built-in GPS, automatic cell network selection, and remote settings adjustments.

The solar bundle comes with the panel, Y2 camera, and two rechargeable battery packs. If you want to keep the upfront cost down, the camera alone is half the price at $125.

According to recent reports, no matter how great your trail camera placement, it’s easy for cameras to miss animals. This is exacerbated in substantial open areas such as wetlands or crop fields where it can be hard to know precisely where animals might appear.

According to recent reports, muddy’s Trifecta 180 is built to minimize these misses. Three motion sensors and a rotating camera capture wide-angle 180-degree images. This is the perfect camera for the edge of large agricultural fields where animals could appear anywhere and often turn up in groups that can be hard to capture in a single image. You have the option for the camera to stitch together impressive panorama images (though they’re harder to appreciate on a phone screen) or the option to capture single-zone images like a regular trail camera would.

According to recent reports, the downside of this impressive device is that it seemed to use more battery power than usual, likely attributable to the camera’s need to move and the usual drains of taking and transmitting images. If you’re planning on running it long-term, I’d consider picking up the solar panel accessory with integrated battery.

Sources indicate that I’ve assembled my choices in this guide based on years of firsthand testing, and I continue testing upcoming trail cam options every season to keep up with the constant rollout of new features and improvements. For decades, I’ve been hanging trail cameras with professional hunters and friends to capture wallowing elk, nursing moose, and scavenging bears on camera.

Historically, I’ve preferred inexpensive, simple cameras that I monitor manually, which keeps my trail camera budget in check, but as connected cameras have gotten more reliable and affordable, I’ve shifted to using cell cams almost exclusively. I hunt in three different states as well as in spots several hours from my home in Colorado, which makes manually checking all my cameras nearly impossible. I still employ “manual” cameras around my property where pulling memory cards frequently isn’t a pain.

According to recent reports, one of the main divisions in the trail camera market is whether your trail camera connects to a cellular network, which, if it does, is what allows you to wirelessly send images over great distances. Connected models are so common now that AT&T and Verizon offer monthly service aims that often come bundled with the camera.

Industry observers note that this connectivity means that you don’t have to physically visit your camera to check out the imagery it has captured—a benefit that’s most tangible when cameras are placed in far-flung hunting spots, but less valuable if you’re using the camera closer to your house. The cellular connection also makes the cameras easier to operate since most cell-connected cameras can be controlled via your smartphone through apps. These allow you to use remote-control camera settings to switch between photo and video modes, adjust camera sensitivity, and check battery levels.

Networked cameras are addictive to use because they can provide instant, or at least frequent, gratification from your camera(s). However, there’s usually a recurring data plan cost in addition to setup complexity. Bottom line: Be sure you really need the connectivity. There also may be legal restrictions on wirelessly connected cameras that limit how you can use them. Be sure to double-check your state’s regulations before buying.

In a recent development, all trail cameras store images locally on the device, whether or not they have the ability to transmit them wirelessly. More often than not, that storage comes in the form of an SD or micro SD card, which you can remove to download your photos. Cameras with wireless support, however, now often feature an internal hard drive, which stores data more reliably, since you no longer need to physically “pull cards” to collect your footage.

If you’re planning to only use a networked camera, I recommend choosing a camera with internal memory. The No. 1 source of problems I’ve had over the years of testing dozens of different trail cameras and helping others set up many more is memory cards. These plastic chip-like cards are fragile, easy to lose, and can be formatted incorrectly. Even when there’s nothing wrong with a card, cheaper SD cards with slower transfer speeds can cause errors when processing larger images and videos.

The only advantage of having a camera with removable memory is if you want to use the camera without a data initiative. This is required for the increasingly rare non-networked cameras, but even connected cameras can be used manually if they have physical cards. Some cameras with internal memory also have an optional SD card slot, such as the Reveal Pro 3.0, which gives you the option to expand storage capacity and use the camera without paying for a data plan.

Sources indicate that this might seem like a minor detail, but given that many people want their trail camera to capture their subjects without alerting those subjects to the camera’s presence, the camera’s exterior color can be a critical factor. Since a majority of trail cameras are marketed to hunters and are intended to be used outdoors, these devices generally come in solid earth tones or camouflage patterns.

In a recent development, if you’re a hunter, you probably already have a good sense of what patterns are most appropriate for your area. If not, snap some photos of the trunks of the trees where you intend to mount the camera; then compare them to the patterns on the cameras you’re considering.

Sources indicate that cameron Shrum, avid bowhunter and co-owner of C&K Archery in Frisco, Colorado, claims, “People will get a good deal on a camera and not realize how crucial it is to have [it] match [their] habitat. The goal is to get pictures of animals without them knowing they are being watched, and when something is out of place, game animals have a tendency to figure it out.”.

Industry observers note that as a professional photographer and videographer, the first thing you need to know about judging the quality of a camera is that there is no single metric that easily tells you which camera will record more clearly. At a glance, checking specs like the number of megapixels in a camera’s sensor gives you a decent clue as to what you can expect.

Ultimately, the best way to gauge the quality of a trail camera is with your eyes. Take a minute to look at sample photos posted by customers on retailers such as Amazon, which give you a practical way to evaluate images taken under natural conditions.

Trail cameras rarely take print-worthy shots, but that isn’t what they’re for. If you’re just patterning animals, image quality isn’t as crucial as simply detecting them. Trophy hunters trying to identify certain calibers of animals or monitor a specific animal across multiple cameras will want to be more picky about image quality and clarity.

Even if you don’t need great fidelity, a better image makes using trail cams more useful and rewarding. I’ve come to appreciate having modern trail cameras that deliver clear images and 4K videos over the crude, fuzzy work of older, lo-fi models.

According to recent reports, I recommend using only lithium batteries in trail cameras. Especially with cheaper cameras, I’ve found that regular alkaline batteries don’t provide enough voltage for the IR flash, and many times a trail camera may not record video with underpowered batteries (alkaline batteries start decreasing in voltage as soon as you start using them). Lithium batteries deliver higher voltage consistently, and they work better in the cold.

If you’re setting up a cellular trail cam, make sure you check signal strength in the area. If you have a camera that offers an app or website (as many now do) that lets you view images on your smartphone, try triggering the camera and see if you receive the notification and image.

Industry observers note that since trail cameras are often left alone for days, weeks, or even months at a time, setting them up properly is notable. Shrum recommends testing your trail camera before you walk away. “Have it snap a few pictures with you walking by and then review them. Sometimes you may not have the right angle; it may be too high or too low. Try to set the height and angle to capture the game in the center of the camera’s view.”.

Trail cameras are usually strapped to a tree and most come packaged with a long strap for this purpose. If you’re placing a camera somewhere without convenient trees for the angle you want, look into a camera stand or even a tripod. Most trail cameras have a standard tripod plate mount (¼-20) and stands or stakes are available from most manufacturers.

Industry observers note that A common spot to place cameras is along well-traveled game trails. A tip I picked up watching champion archer Levi Morgan put up cameras on one of his hunting leases: rather than pointing the camera down a trail where it’s likely to be in the line-of-sight of animals as they walk it, put the camera off-trail between 10 and 30 feet away perpendicular to the trail. This will usually give you broadside images of animals instead of head-on and puts the camera in their periphery.

Recent findings suggest that once you’ve tested your placement (and image transmission for connected cameras) by viewing a test photo on the app or the camera itself, scan the camera’s field of view for latest-growth vegetation. Plants and tree branches can result in a near-constant stream of false triggers on a windy day. I like to place any plants or branches I cut behind the camera for a bit of concealment, making sure they can’t blow in front of the camera.

Industry observers note that since trail cams are motion-activated, a fast trigger seems vital. You don’t want an animal to pass by the camera before you get a photo, right? In my experience, the real problem is taking the photo too quickly, which results in seeing just the nose of a slow-moving deer. Still, many brands tout their fast trigger speeds as if they solve an important problem.

It has been revealed that “It’s kind of a BS spec, frankly,” Gregg Farrell, vice president of marketing for Tactacam Reveal, told me. “The goal is to capture the animal in the center of the frame and our cameras do that through the operating system working with the [motion] sensor.”.

Most trail cameras have listed trigger speeds around a half second, which can work well, but are often too quick if implemented poorly. I almost always switch my cameras to shoot a multishot burst, if available, to give the camera more opportunities to grab a well-framed shot. Keep in mind, though, that this will double or triple the number of images you receive, so it may not be a solution if you’re using a cell-connected camera and trying to save with a limited-data plan.

In a recent development, some cameras have detection delay settings that let you set a period of time after an image is captured before it’ll take another. This can cut down on look-alike images if an animal is hanging around in the detection area, especially if you’ve enabled a multishot mode.

According to recent reports, connected trail cameras make scouting convenient, but they come with hidden costs. Almost all cellular trail cameras require a monthly data strategy to cover the cost of cloud storage and image transmission.

In a recent development, many companies tack on extra fees for features such as live streaming, which eat up a lot of data and cost the companies money with their network provider partners. Like sitting at a blackjack table, it’s easy to get caught up in the excitement of scouting and click your way to hundreds of dollars in recurring monthly charges. You can review the details of each tech giant’s data aims before you buy and decide what features you want to use in advance. You can save money on a camera if you decide you don’t need all the latest features and avoid the temptation of activating those extra charges in the process.

It has been revealed that common game animals such as whitetail deer and elk tend to settle into routines during the summer months which often persist into early fall. The change of seasons and seasonal mating windows will help throw routine out the window in the fall, but if you can identify high-traffic areas in the spring and early summer, that will likely continue all summer.

In a recent development, the best practices for finding a good spot and setting up the camera properly are the same in any season. Spring in some ways makes it easier to identify animal travel patterns since the ground is often wet and recent activity is more obvious. Hike your zone and look for fresh signs to identify intersections, pinch points, and frequently visited locations. If you’re able to access your cameras easily and often, use the early season to experiment with different locations for a few weeks and try fresh spots you hadn’t considered before that show promise based on animal signs. Half the fun of placing these cameras is finding that perfect location and image framing that yields a ton of exciting wildlife images.

In a recent development, there are plenty of things that can trigger a trail camera other than the type(s) of animals you’re looking to capture, including squirrels, lights, and vegetation moving in the wind. “False triggers,” as we call them, are not only disappointing, but waste storage and burn through your data plan. It’s hard to eliminate them completely, but there are lots of ways to minimize them.

The most important is proper camera setup. Once you’ve got it framed up the way you want and have a successful test image, look for branches and weeds in the frame, primarily in the foreground. A single goldenrod stalk or pine bough can burn through a month’s data allotment on a windy day, so take your time to clear the immediate area in front of your camera.

You can’t always clear cut in front of a camera, so if you find you’re still getting more false triggers than you’d like, adjust the camera’s trigger sensitivity down. Many cameras only offer high or low, but if you have a more finely graded adjustment such as the 1 through 10 sensitivity settings on the Reveal Pro 3.0, adjust slowly down until you stop getting false triggers so you don’t overcorrect and miss animals.

Some cameras also use recognition software to reject images that appear to be empty. Moultrie’s Edge cameras allow you to only accept motion triggers in selected zones of an image, effectively blocking triggers from, for example, a corner of a detection zone with moving tree branches.

Most states have some sort of regulation with the use of trail cameras, especially when used on public land and as they relate to hunting activities. Arizona, where game animals tend to congregate around limited water sources, banned trail cameras for hunting statewide in 2021. Colorado, where I live, has few restrictions on trail camera use before your hunting season begins, but limits employing them while you’re actively hunting.

Using trail cameras on your own private property doesn’t usually involve too many restrictions, but be sure to check the regulations from your state’s wildlife management organization to confirm, as private land practices can still be regulated through the hunting codes since wildlife are considered a shared public resource.

There are so many options for security cameras dedicated to home use, and because of that, most of the time it makes more sense to just buy a security camera from a brand that specializes in that application, such as Ring or Google Nest.

Recent findings suggest that these products generally have superior apps and software to hunt-focused trail cameras. Since they're designed for home use, they effortlessly connect to your home WiFi network, don’t require a data subscription, and will have features trail cameras won’t such as two-way communication.

That said, if you already own trail cameras and don’t need specific features, most trail cameras can serve a security purpose. The best trail cameras to employ for security are the newer “live” trail cameras that transmit imagery instantly via cell networks and notify you on your phone when the camera has been triggered.

Another option is WiFi-enabled trail cameras that can connect to your phone without a cellular network to transmit images. However, these cameras don’t usually transmit if you’re not within range of the camera (i.e., at home), so they’re limited to general monitoring rather than real-time notification when you’re away.

Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept.
  • Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.
  • According to recent reports, sources noted Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who presently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

According to recent reports, sources noted Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who presently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Recent findings suggest that senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”.

According to recent reports, the post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Sources indicate that homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

According to recent reports, paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”.

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Recent findings suggest that clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”.

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this vital position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Recent findings suggest that collins remarked in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”.

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

The Golden Rules of Affordable Family Travel, Illustrated by Mona Chalabi

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, my first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014.
  • According to recent reports, take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions.
  • Sources indicate that as we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in Fresh York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, my first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014. I had moved to the US in March of that year and had planned on working from home until a friend generously invited me to go spend the day with her family; an act of unguarded openness that I’ve realized is one of the many things that differentiates Americans from Brits. As soon as we got off the train in Cambridge, Massachusetts, I realized that even though my friend lived in a nasty, overcrowded apartment in Brooklyn, she came from a family that had immense wealth. After dinner, as I helped wash plates in the kitchen, my friend’s mum asked her why she wouldn’t just move into the lovely building they had bought for her. She turned beet red and handed me another dirty plate without looking at me.

According to recent reports, take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions. Of course, there’s the annual reminder of colonization which requires a careful forgetting of the people who have been colonized. And then there’s the financial aspect of it. At first blush, it seems like the least capitalist holiday of the year—there isn’t the expense of Christmas or Hanukkah gift-giving or the extravagance of Halloween candy. Yet the holiday also marks the start of one of the year's busiest travel seasons when families are taking great expense to reunite, vacation, and explore outside of their every day lives.

Sources indicate that as we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in Fresh York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe. All of these stories say something about the wealth of the person writing it, whether or not they wanted to reveal that information. I’m obsessed with getting to the truth about someone’s class (it’s why I wrote my book on the subject), and so these family dispatches, which serve as equal parts advice and confession, are a treat I’ll come back to when I’m not busy washing a rich family’s plates. —Mona Chalabi, Pulitzer Prize-winning writer and illustrator.

Keep reading for the tips and tricks of affordable family travel, road-tested by the experts and illustrated by Mona Chalabi.

In a recent development, I know the secret to parenting and I’m willing to share it: snacks. Snacks are everything—they’re an activity, a mood changer, and a window into culture for kids. Hit a local farmers market on your first day or if you’re somewhere truly out of their comfort zone even a local convenience store—like 7-Eleven in Tokyo—for something that can feel both familiar and novel. If your hotel room has a refrigerator you can store any pre-cut fruit that you buy, or opt for items that don’t require refrigeration like apples, bananas, and clementines. Bring a lightweight backpack, refill each morning, and watch the hangry meltdowns (mostly) vanish. —Dana Kravis, global executive director, CNT video.

In a recent development, last December in London, we stayed in a quaint Airbnb in Primrose Hill and explored different neighborhoods on foot. When our kids, then eight and three, got tired, we hopped on a double-decker bus and headed upstairs, hoping for front seats. Suddenly, getting home became an amusement park ride: Christmas lights, bustling streets, panoramic views. The kids loved it; as a photographer, I loved the vantage point. London caps daily bus fares when you use the same card or phone, and children under 11 ride free. We’ve done this in Singapore, too. Our rule: skip the sightseeing tour (or Uber) and make public transportation part of the family adventure. —Tanveer Badal, photographer.

In a recent development, breakfast is where family vacations are made, or broken. My moody teenagers can’t be pried out of bed no matter what city they wake up in, so instead of wringing my uncaffeinated hands and hoping to get us all on the same schedule, I just bring my own breakfast, coffee included. Whether in Paris, Rome, or a tent, you will find me hand-grinding my coffee beans, brewing a pour-over, and snacking on a pastry left over from the previous day while I peruse headlines. Avoiding the time and expense of a sit-down breakfast, and indulging in a bit of morning self-care, means we can focus on the adventures and meals we are actually going to remember. —Chris Morocco, food director of Bon Appétit and Epicurious.

My parents and I meet in Aruba every winter for a family vacation that’s warm and relaxing when everyone else is cold and miserable. It’s a classic only child/parents trip where we spend most of our time eating lunch talking about where we’re going to eat dinner. We spend our days mostly just reading parallel to each other. I’ve never been an e-reader user, so I have to bring several physical books to read to get me through the week. The key is that my mom and I have some shared taste in books, so when we finish our own we can swap and save ourselves buying extra books (or lugging even heavier luggage through the airport). —Alison Leiby, comedian and writer.

Finding creative ways to entertain wiggly one-year-olds with limited attention spans can be daunting, but it turns out all you need is a good window. From London to California, staying in rooms on low floors with windows overlooking lots of activity below has resulted in seemingly endless engagement—waving at commuters striding by or golfers strolling a few feet away? Bonus points if the room has curtains with electronic controls—that guarantees an extra hour of ooohs and aaahs, at least. —Sarah Khan, contributing editor.

I have a thing for seeing “The World’s Biggest or Oldest,” and so here we were at Missouri’s Oldest Wooden Suspension Bridge. “Don’t tell your mom,” I said to my kids, because any bridge that was built from wood during the Civil War should be treated with caution—and, also, all good dad stories start that way. We started up the van, piled everyone in, and began the adventure. The wood cracked and echoed as we drove over the river. It sounded like a popping spinal cord. We swayed, and for a moment, I actually questioned myself. I should have just taken them to the park. Thankfully, I can now confidently say that Missouri’s oldest wooden suspension bridge can hold the weight of a mini-van. —Shannon Carpenter, humorist.

Upcoming York is an expensive city and the best way to keep it cheap is to throw petty cash at it. Instead of buying tickets to an overpriced kid’s experience, I give my children a few twenty dollar bills and take them to Chinatown for a shopping spree. They love the atrocious arcade, and there are fake Labubus, squishy dumplings, a plastic “jade” green dragon that my son now keeps on his bedside, and a 'gold' necklace my daughter thinks is treasure. —Stephanie Danler, author.

As a seasoned travel writer, I know that any hotel that’s gotten media coverage is often pushing $1,000/night. My trick for affordable family lodging is loading up Google maps, figuring out which area we’re going to stay in, and picking a cheerful place with good reviews in the $250 range. It’s almost never one you’ve heard of, but they’re always clean and cheerful, usually family-owned, and we always leave with big hugs and promises to keep in touch. That doesn’t happen at the Georges V. My kids (12 and 8) loved a converted windmill in Rome, a townhouse two blocks from the Rijksmuseum and—most recently—an orange grove near Siracusa where they spent so much time chasing the owner’s cats they even forgot Wi-Fi existed. A steal at any price! —Priyanka Mattoo, filmmaker and author.

People tell you about a million things you “need” before your baby is born, but there's one that has come in the most handy, and I've had a true love/hate relationship with it since day one: A travel car seat. After a ton of research—some may say over-research—we bought a Maxi Cosi Romi. It's rated high for safety, but it's also easy to strap into a car and also an airplane. We always bring it on the airplane, and that's where the headache comes in. While the Maxi Cosi Romi is considered lightweight, it's also massive and bulky, and the only way to get it through the airport and onto the plane is by wearing it in a special backpack. I'm pretty sure that I'm one of the most annoying people in any airport as I'm walking through it since I can't really see if I'm bumping into people in the TSA line or getting to the gate. The thing is that, after I considered the numbers, it's actually a really wise investment because most rental car places charge anywhere from $10 to $15 a day to rent a car seat, so we've already started saving money because of it. Now, that's about a hundred or more dollars we're not spending when we go out of town and bring the Maxi. It's wildly annoying and inconvenient, and I look like I'm wearing a jetpack as I'm walking through the airport, but it's worth it. —Jason Diamond, 'Figuring' family columnist at The Cut.

Recent findings suggest that I️ live in Brooklyn where people leave really good stuff out on the street. Once I️ found one of those giant extra storage containers you put on top of your car. I️ haven't found the time to figure out how to put it on top of the car; it's been taking up valuable space in my home for over a year. The other day, I️ found another one that looked even fancier. I️ dragged it home. One day, ideally before our car gets too old to work anymore, I️ will figure this out, then get rid of the extra one somehow (do I️ need to call 311?). After that, my husband, our two kids, our dog, our parakeets and I️ will pack up everything we could possibly need to rent a house somewhere for a week or two. I️ have my eye on Block Island or Martha's Vineyard. —Liana Finck, cartoonist and author.

From bustling markets to neighborhood festivals, I've learned that some of the best family entertainment happens in the streets. In Oaxaca, my four-year-old was mesmerized by calendas, raucous community processions with brass bands, towering puppets called monos de calenda, and rag-covered revelers known as tiliches. Paradegoers tossed my kid candy, fireworks exploded overhead, and the party raged late into the night. We didn't pay a peso. Before booking pricey family activities, research local festivals, celebrations, and public performances. Sometimes the most exciting show in town is happening right on the sidewalk. —Ashlea Halpern, contributing editor.

On our last family vacation to Rajasthan, a passionfruit lassi from our five-star hotel nearly ruined the trip. We’re talking emergency roadside bathroom stops and several days of Zofran. We’ve been taking our kids—Vijay, Vik, and Meera—to Rajasthan since they were babies; they’re teenagers now. And we’ve learned one unexpected lesson: the sickest we’ve ever been in India was after eating at our five-star hotel. More than once.

So we’ve adopted a new philosophy: pack the right medicine and embrace street food. In Jaipur, Vineet Sharma, founder of Jaipur Walks, led us on a street food tour around the bustling market, introducing us to piping-hot pyaaz kachori and creamy, saffron-rich kulfi. His advice? Choose clean stalls with high turnover, and favor food cooked fresh and served hot over raw offerings. At busy stalls, food is often prepared continuously and served straight from the heat—sometimes a more reassuring bet than a meal at a luxury hotel or high-end restaurant. And if your stomach’s going to revolt, at least make the meal memorable. —Christine Chitnis, author and photographer.

In a recent development, this may not be the most popular piece of advice, and I doubt it'll be the most obvious: take your kids overseas during school time. Hear me out: the longer you can stretch your child's travels beyond the limited school holidays when ticket prices always soar, the better for your wallet. Of course, every parent needs to set their own boundary on what and how much school their kind can miss in the name of travel but I feel, especially at a young age, the benefits of the trip outweigh the additional days in the classroom. As I am writing this, I am preparing to leave tomorrow with my first grader for Italy for a week. We are cooking up plans to take our two kids on a long haul trip to the southern hemisphere that'll cut into a week of school. I have heard from more than one expert that Disney especially, should be done when your kids are young, and outside normal school holidays if you want to get great value. I don't do it often but I do balance the guilt with rules—we have to read every day, and do exercises from a homework packet to keep on top of the basics. One day, and soon, I know I won't want to do this much more. But for now, I'm taking every chance to do so. —Erin Florio, global features director.

  • The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.
  • The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

It has been revealed that “The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition notes.

Recent findings suggest that trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Recent findings suggest that immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”.

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

In a recent development, the case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

Industry observers note that rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Recent findings suggest that colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

Recent findings suggest that the red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

According to recent reports, discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Explanation: What is blocking the center of the Milky Way? During its 13 billion years, our Milky Way has collected a lot of dust. In contrast to the skin cells, dirt, pollen, and other debris that make up the dust behind your couch, cosmic dust is hundreds of times smaller and made of tiny compounds of oxygen, carbon, and other elements released into space when a star dies. Today’s video reveals infrared light from the Milky Way’s center gathered by NASA’s SPHEREx satellite. Each false color in the video corresponds to the infrared color associated with the wavelength shown in the top left. In the near-infrared, like 1.2 microns, light gets absorbed and scatters off of dust particles. SPHEREx then sees the Galactic Center almost entirely blocked by clouds of dust. In the mid-infrared, though, light is able to pierce through the dust and reach SPHEREx. This is similar to, but not exactly, why sunsets are red!Tomorrow's picture: a sandy view of the Milky Way.

NASA’s Hubble Views Ocean of Stars in Groundwork for Roman

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An expanse of stars gleams in a rainbow of colors in these NASA Hubble Space Telescope images of the Milky Way.
  • Astronomers study the Milky Way’s galactic bulge because it holds nearly a quarter of the galaxy’s stellar mass, and its proximity allows them to examine the region in greater detail.
  • According to recent reports, hubble views the universe primarily in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light, while Roman collects data in near-infrared light and some visible light.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An expanse of stars gleams in a rainbow of colors in these NASA Hubble Space Telescope images of the Milky Way. The images focus on an area of sky toward the galactic bulge, a densely packed, spherical region of stars that surrounds the center of a galaxy’s disk. These Hubble observations are part of a survey that will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope observations as they seek to characterize the stars and search for exoplanets in this busy region of our galaxy.

Astronomers study the Milky Way’s galactic bulge because it holds nearly a quarter of the galaxy’s stellar mass, and its proximity allows them to examine the region in greater detail. Although we can see the glow from these crowded spheres of stars in other galaxies, they are too jam-packed and far away to resolve individual stars. By studying the Milky Way’s galactic bulge, researchers hope to find newly introduced planets and better understand how galaxies form, evolve, and interact over billions of years.

According to recent reports, hubble views the universe primarily in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light, while Roman collects data in near-infrared light and some visible light. Because researchers wish to compare Hubble’s observations to future Roman observations, Hubble looked at the region in wavelengths that overlap with Roman’s areas of sensitivity, the red end of the visible spectrum and near-infrared wavelengths.

Hubble’s high resolution allows its instruments to collect data on the brightness, ages, composition, and motion of stars over time. With this knowledge, astronomers can search for potential exoplanets, determine the location of black holes or dark matter, and better understand our galaxy’s environment and evolution.

In a recent development, A key component of Roman’s future observations is the search for exoplanets by capturing microlensing events, a type of gravitational lensing that occurs when light from a more distant object is magnified and distorted by the mass of a closer object along the line of sight. The way light from the distant star is distorted and magnified can reveal clues to the nature of the foreground star and any planets it may have. Hubble's observations will help characterize stars in the region before they undergo a lensing event. Months or years in the future, when Roman captures a microlensing event, researchers can compare Hubble data to Roman data of the event, making it easer to interpret. These microlensing events are on a much smaller scale, that of stars and planets, than larger gravitational lenses that occur around galaxies and galaxy clusters.

Over Hubble’s lifetime, it has observed our galaxy’s central bulge many times. These legacy surveys include the WFC3 Galactic Bulge Treasury Program that used Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 to study the brightness, precise positions, and motions of stars in this congested part of our galaxy. It also includes the Sagittarius Window Eclipsing Extrasolar Planet Search (SWEEPS) that used Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys to look at 180,000 stars in the bulge of our galaxy. These new observations come from an observing program (#17776: S. Terry) designed to aid Roman in its search for exoplanets, black holes, neutron stars, and more. The data also adds to Hubble’s continuing legacy of high-precision observations of stars in the galactic bulge.

Claire AndreoliNASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MDclaire.andreoli@nasa.gov.

Since its 1990 launch, the Hubble Space Telescope has changed our fundamental understanding of the universe.

Hubble's most notable scientific discoveries reflect the broad range of research and the breakthroughs it has achieved.

NASA's Hubble and Roman space telescopes will work together to broaden our perspective of the universe.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will settle essential questions in the areas of dark energy, exoplanets, and astrophysics.

NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth.
  • Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers.
  • According to recent reports, while space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly crucial as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet.

According to recent reports, while space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A fresh investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.

Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating.

Researchers at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries.

Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions.

Industry observers note that delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation.

Sources indicate that but looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft.

Many crops have been grown in space, but none so far have come from the gourd family. Cucumbers could be the first.

It has been revealed that before crops like cucumbers can be grown and eaten in space, they must undergo extensive testing. NASA-funded researchers recently evaluated cucumbers for their growth, yield, and nutrition under spaceflight conditions.

The researchers found that while the plants showed some signs of enlarged leaves, they produced a steady stream of edible fruit, according to a study published in August in the journal HortScience.

Offering a variety of crops, such as cucumbers, not only benefits astronauts’ diets and mental well-being, but it also increases plant biodiversity, which can improve the likelihood of crop success on long-duration missions.

Herbs can spice up life in space, turning a bland meal into a bold one.

Lemon basil, an edible herb with a citrus scent and taste, is making strides in testing at NASA Kennedy.

According to recent reports, researchers report that lemon basil passed its preliminary round of space crop testing and successfully underwent seed sanitization, which is required before spaceflight to remove microorganisms from the seeds. Lemon basil’s next steps include assessing its growth in plant pillows, which can house plants aboard the space station.

Menu fatigue can quickly become a problem for astronauts, but fresh herbs like lemon basil help transform packaged meals into something new and satisfying, supporting human health and performance in space.

Recent findings suggest that NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand indicated me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”.

Industry observers note that I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

According to recent reports, it’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

In a recent development, well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.).

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:.

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

Recent findings suggest that but this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

Recent findings suggest that I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

It has been revealed that additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you strategy to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

Sources indicate that so I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

According to recent reports, the paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

According to recent reports, but does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

Industry observers note that the gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

It has been revealed that for this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this tech giant, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.).

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:.

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment stated the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

In a recent development, the worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or problems with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most notable things to have perfect on your application.

Recent findings suggest that once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.).

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s crucial that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!
