📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that air France delivered one of the best business class flights I have taken in years on my journey from Paris to New York. The new A350-900 cabin is excellent, but what impressed me most was how well everything came together, from the comfortable seat to the delicious dinner, gracious service, and fast Starlink Wi-Fi.

In a recent development, I shared my first impressions of this flight earlier, calling it the best business class experience in Europe. Having had more time to reflect on it, I stand by that assessment…this flight left very little room for improvement.

I needed to return to the United States after taking my children to Germany for the summer. Flying Blue came through with a last-minute business class award from Basel to Paris to Latest York for 60,000 miles plus €453 in taxes and fees. The timing worked perfectly and I booked this about 36-hour before departure, so saver space can certainly open up via FlyingBlue.

It has been revealed that this was a so-called “reverse redeye,” leaving Europe late in the evening and arriving in the United States even later that same evening. That suited my plans very well, particularly because I had an overnight drive to Pittsburgh ahead of me after landing.

Industry observers note that my journey began in Basel with an Air France Hop! flight to Paris. I had time to visit the lounge before my connection and enjoyed a meal there, though I deliberately left room for dinner onboard.

Industry observers note that stepping onboard, I found my seat in 6L. Though approaching 8:00 pm, it was still very light outside.

I first reviewed Air France A350 business class in 2020, flying from Paris to Toronto. I enjoyed that flight very much, but the newer business class cabin represents a substantial improvement.

Industry observers note that the business class cabin has 48 seats spread over a front and rear cabin. These seats are based on the Stelia Opera platform and are arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration, with every passenger having direct aisle access and a sliding door to provide additional privacy.

According to recent reports, far more crucial the gimmicky door was the room for your feet, which I found plentiful. Legroom is 43 inches when the seat is the upright position and it transforms into a bed that is 79 inches long. Seats are 21 inches wide.

It has been revealed that there are no personal art vents, but thankfully the cabin was kept very chilly. I also loved the window darkening feature, where the window tinting could be adjusted simply by sliding your finger left or right.

I found this suite spacious and comfortable whether sitting upright, reclining, or lying down. The cabin looks so sharp. I particularly love the illuminated winged seahorse at each seat…a small detail, but one that gives the cabin an unmistakable Air France identity.

There was plenty of personal storage, and the wireless charging worked well, though there was also USB-C and universal A/C power.

After dinner, I converted my seat into a bed and slept for about four hours.

The Sofitel-branded bedding (duvet, mattress pad, pillow) was excellent, and I found the seat very comfortable for sleeping.

This is one of my favorite business class seats.

Sources indicate that air France provided a very attractive amenity kit with an embossed seahorse on the bag. It was lined with red and the contents included:.

Sources indicate that the catering was a highlight of this flight. I had eaten in the lounge, but was very glad I saved room for dinner.

Before takeoff, flight attendants offered Champagne and a warm towel, along with the familiar Gavottes savory biscuits.

The full menu (every menu item and ingredient is French except for Coca-Cola):.

Dinner began with an appetizer of pea, lemon, and basil cream accompanied by smoked salmon fillet and raspberry and grapefruit jelly.

A side salad accompanied the starter, though I saved mine until after the main course, as the French do. The bread was delicious.

Recent findings suggest that I also tried the Quintessence cocktail, an Air France variation on a Negroni. It combined La Quintinye royal red vermouth, bitter Chambéry liqueur, a hint of fig, and ABK6 VSOP Cognac. I enjoyed it very much. It was not nearly as strong as a traditional Negroni, which suited me just fine on this flight.

For my main course, I chose veal with a creamy morel mushroom sauce, spelt risotto, and peas.

Admittedly, the presentation was not going to win any awards…yes, it looked like vomit. But it tasted delicious and I would happily order it again. I enjoyed a delicious glass of Chateau D’Arsac wine, which was so good.

A cheese course followed, then dessert. I enjoyed both ice cream and a crispy hazelnut tart, accompanied by hot chocolate.

This was a substantial supper and a very satisfying one.

About an hour before landing, flight attendants served a light meal of shrimp with a pickled cucumber salad.

It was excellent and just the right amount of food after the large dinner. I had two espressos with it, which helped prepare me for the late night ahead.

It has been revealed that the entertainment system included a tail camera, which I particularly enjoyed during our departure from Paris (though not the fire that seemed to be burning near CDG). It was a gorgeous evening, and watching the aircraft leave Charles de Gaulle was a lovely way to begin the flight.

I did not watch any movies or TV on this flight, but there was large selection of movies, TV reveals, games, and music.

Noise-cancelling headphones were provided, though you can also connect your own Bluetooth device.

Fast, free Starlink internet was available onboard. The connection worked from gate to gate and felt much like using the internet on the ground. I did not have any essential work to complete on this flight, but I appreciated being able to connect onboard. Starlink increasingly influences which flights I book. Air France already gives me plenty of reasons to choose it, but reliable internet makes the proposition even more attractive, especially for a daytime westbound journey when I might otherwise spend several hours working.

The Air France A350 has three lavatories in business class: one I the front (though typically reserved for crew use) and two in between the front and rear cabin.

Service was warm and attentive throughout the flight. I was even addressed by surname.

According to recent reports, I have heard plenty of complaints over the years about service on Air France, but my own experiences have been very positive. This crew continued that pattern and the great service complemented the rest of the experience. I enjoyed a delicious meal, slept comfortably, and felt well cared for throughout the journey.

According to recent reports, the latest seat deserves attention, but a cabin can only do so much without a good crew in terms of leaving a lasting positive impression. On this flight, Air France delivered both.

We landed on time at JFK, and I promptly cleared immigration using Global Entry. The late arrival had been part of the appeal when booking, and the flight delivered exactly what I had hoped for: an enjoyable evening onboard, a few hours of rest, and an on-time arrival in Newly introduced York.

Then it was time to collect a rental car and begin my overnight drive to Pittsburgh….

This was a tremendous flight on Air France…I have no complaints at all about anything.

I liked the older A350 business class product when I flew it in 2020, but the newer seat is a considerable improvement. Pair that with excellent bedding, delicious food, and a gracious crew, then add Starlink, and I struggle to identify much that I would change. Cappuccinos maybe that are not powdered?

The lack of individual air vents remains a drawback, though the comfortable cabin temperature thankfully meant it did not interfere with my sleep on this flight.

It has been revealed that air France reminded me how enjoyable a transatlantic business class flight can be when the airline gets the details right. I would happily book this product again and would go out of my way to find it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

In a recent development, outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

Industry observers note that the gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

According to recent reports, in a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he stated when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Problem One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he stated, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

In a recent development, zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It has been revealed that it marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

Recent findings suggest that the Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with looks to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

It has been revealed that zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services tech giant Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a manufacturer registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron noted.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s tech giant, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which indicates it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

It has been revealed that in 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail mentioned about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this Thanksgiving, I keep thinking about the last days of Narnia. Not because I believe the world is ending, but because C.S. Lewis understood how easily faith can be exploited by those seeking power…and how difficult it becomes to see clearly when we are frightened or angry.

In The Last Battle, an ape named Shift dresses a donkey in a lion’s skin and persuades the Narnians that Aslan has returned. Shift then speaks for him, demanding obedience and using their love for Aslan to advance his own interests.

The deception works because the Narnians want to be faithful. They have difficulty believing that someone invoking Aslan could be asking them to betray everything Aslan represents.

In a recent development, I find that painfully familiar when I watch Christians excuse conduct in Donald Trump that they would rightly condemn in almost anyone else. Once defending a leader becomes a religious obligation, we have given him something that never belonged to him.

Recent findings suggest that the lion’s skin does not make the donkey Aslan. Invoking Christianity does not make a political demand Christian.

That warning applies to me too. Seeing another person’s hypocrisy does not excuse my own contempt. Being right about a political failure does not make every word I write about it righteous.

It has been revealed that I can become so occupied with what is wrong that I stop noticing what God has given me. I can begin to enjoy indignation. That is a dangerous habit for anyone, particularly someone who writes for a living.

Scripture takes ingratitude seriously. In Romans 1:21, Paul describes people who knew God but neither honored Him as God nor gave thanks. Ingratitude accompanies their descent into darkened thinking and idolatry. And in Ephesians 5:3–4, Paul places thanksgiving where corrupt speech ought to be displaced. Gratitude is part of how we resist sin.

Recent findings suggest that giving thanks reminds me that I am a recipient of mercy. I have no grounds to treat another person as beyond its reach.

I remain grateful to be an American. I will continue to criticize our government when I believe it deserves criticism, and I will continue to pray for those who govern us, including President Trump.

But my allegiance belongs to the Kingdom of Heaven and to Jesus Christ, the King of Kings. No party gets to borrow that allegiance. No president gets to claim it.

Recent findings suggest that that gives me freedom to acknowledge something good done by someone I oppose and something wrong done by someone I supported. It also means an election cannot deliver everything I hope for or take away everything that matters.

In a recent development, paul tells Christians to give thanks in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18). I understand that to include circumstances I want to change. Gratitude does not require pretending that injustice is good or that incompetence is harmless.

Recent findings suggest that today, I am thankful for my wife and children, for the church that has sustained me, my loving and supportive family and friends, and for the extraordinary privilege of traveling through this world and sharing it with you. Most of all, I am thankful that my hope rests with a King whose character does not require excuses.

Lewis understood that Shift did not have the last word. I need to remember that too.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that occasionally, a place will take hold of our collective imagination in much the same way that an unsolved mathematical problem does, or a treasure hunt, or an ancient, coded message found moldering in an attic, beguiling with its mystery, difficulty, and promise of a reward. Few places exert quite this pull like the Congo Basin, a thick block of forest and rivers covering much of Central Africa, home to some 150 ethnic groups, and a raft of extraordinary biodiversity. Despite its size and its importance as a counterbalance to climate change, the region endures a dearth of scientific research funding and conservation efforts. Roughly the size of India, it has inspired and vexed many visitors (even those who might otherwise have claimed to have conquered it).

A floating village in the Congo River Basin.

Sources indicate that the idea could be mentioned to originate in the late 19th century, as Europeans made their way into the great forests seeking fortune and glory. The Welsh explorer Henry Morton Stanley, the first to leave a detailed record of his journey across the Basin, claimed that even after a three-year trek (1874-77) it remained “a region of fable and mystery.” That was exactly the mix sought by Polish sailor Józef Korzeniowski, who, as a boy, looked at the map of Africa, then a white space, and “declared that some day I would go there.” Eventually, and not long after Stanley, he did, and with the captaincy of a steamboat on the Congo River, was tasked with collecting one Mr. Klein, an upcountry agent employed by the brutal Belgian trading company. Korzeniowski was horrified by what he saw along the river—colonization and resource extraction at its cruelest and bloodiest—calling it “the vilest scramble for loot that ever disfigured the history of human conscience and geographical exploration.” Later, Józef Korzeniowski became Joseph Conrad, Mr. Klein became Mr. Kurtz, and the rest is literary history.

Dzanga Baï, a protected area in the southwestern Central African Republic also known as “the village of elephants.”.

The latest journeyman to apply themself to the region is another Welshman, Ash Dykes, whose TikTok videos of his journey paddling down the Sangha River (a tributary of the mighty Congo River) have received millions of views. By mid-October, Dykes, who calls himself an extreme athlete, was midway through the 400 miles he hoped to cover. His videos—the anxiety and speculation of his preparation; the amplification of the danger en route—are over-exaggerated, designed to amuse his audience; they are spectacle. Looking bewildered in his state-of-the-art inflatable boat, Dykes is most often met by competent, unaffected locals, paddling their wooden pirogues with balletic grace. And brave though Dykes certainly is, most of what he has accomplished—attending a hunt with the Ba’aka people, seeing the forest elephants in Dzanga Baï, or tracking Western lowland gorillas—can be done by just about anyone.

The Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions, is the basin's only passenger cruise.

Recent findings suggest that I, too, was one enchanted by the inscrutability of the Congo Basin, and I dreamt of one day traveling along its rivers and into its forests; in my mind’s eye, I envisioned dusk slipping into night, to the rhythm of a pounding drumbeat. Not long ago, I departed Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of Congo, aboard the Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions. As the only such passenger vessel in the Congo Basin, the crew of the Ngalessa is accustomed to receiving rarefied looks from the riverbank. But just as often, the ship’s approach was greeted with aplomb, for it was an event in the villages and brought goods, along with community support and news from away.

Sources indicate that in comparison to the coarse and crowded daka-dakas—flat-topped river barges, stuffed with goods and spewing black, acrid smoke as they chunter between Kinshasa and Kisangani—those of us onboard the Ngalessa traveled in glorious comfort: air-conditioning, three square meals a day, and private bathrooms. We also had the benefit of our local guides and their familiarity with the languages, customs, and faces up and down the river. This included, in the riverside village of Ngabe, the appearance of an Ejengi, a forest spirit made of palm fronds that danced and spun as a crowd of onlookers sang, drummed, and screamed in delight.

“Don’t worry,” our guide noted. “Look at his dusty bare feet!” Elsewhere, we watched an Indigenous Luma woman cut, strip, and chew twigs into a pulp that could be used as medicinal pain relief. On other days, we kayaked through the flooded forests of the Alima River, and traded with fishermen who brought their slim pirogues against our mammoth ship to hand over smoked fish and fruit.

Kayaking through the flooded forests of the Alima River.

Eight days and 600 miles after leaving Brazzaville, we arrived at the outpost of Ouesso on the Sangha River. I journeyed further upon that water by launch boat, into the Central African Republic, and spent days at Sangha Lodge, drinking gin and tonics with local legend Rod Cassidy, an eco-tourism pioneer who has spent years living and working with the local Ba’aka people. It was through him I had the good luck to attend a hunt with those same Ba’aka, and to look on while they divvied up the duiker they snagged in their homemade nets. Afterwards, they whooped and hollered as they carried the meat out and into their village—a feast!

In a recent development, in the heightened state of travel, there comes occasionally a moment like falling into an empty space and, as two glancing stones can spark a blaze, a light of comprehension is illuminated. Sometimes this moment manifests itself as love, other times as admiration, or confusion. Conrad left the Congo in spiritual, psychological, and physical shock. “Before the Congo, I was a mere animal,” he wrote after his consequential journey. He was changed, as travelers who go forward with their ears and eyes open (to say nothing of their hearts) are changed. Watching the Ba’aka poised in their hunt, ears tilted to the slightest sound, I felt myself see humanity as it had existed since time immemorial. As they laughed and chatted on their success, the women showing their fangs (chipped with rocks as a show of strength), and the men slapping each other on the back, I could barely remember seeing such happiness elsewhere.

The Congo Basin may still be raw and atavistic—great adventures there are still possible—but it is no “heart of darkness” (a title which for Conrad lay not in the location itself, but rather mankind’s ability to exploit and vilify others). What separates it from other places is its independence. It requires protection, yes, but has no need, and few provisions, for any prying visitors; it is not a prize to be conquered. Most incredibly, it remains the home of peoples who have not yet latched themselves to tourism; people who sustain themselves almost wholly from an expanse of forest and the waters that for others can only be the basis of wonder and amazement. And yet, after all the sorrow and misery that colonialism brought to the Congo Basin, the people remain sincere and earnest, and willing to show others the best of their land.

A lone kayaker glides underneath a hazy sky.

According to recent reports, one night, as the Ngalessa drifted northward, from beneath the awning on the ship’s upper deck, I watched a cloud bank clump and darken. Finally, with an incision of lightning, the downpour came, brief but fierce. The sun returned, low in the sky but still warm, and the scent of damp earth rose up. A patter of drumming reached us from somewhere, before being swallowed by the forest. The dinner bell rang, and I thought I never want this trip to end.

The 11 Most Beautiful Beaches in the Caribbean

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs.
  • Industry observers note that barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here.
  • In a recent development, grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs. Nearly every island has a stretch of powdery sand and improbably blue water, and after a while, the “nice sand, nice water” trope stops registering at all. We’re talking beauty in the transcendental sense—the kind of beauty that makes you feel something. Maybe it’s a crescent of sand more pink than you thought could happen in nature. Maybe it’s a labyrinth of granite boulders spilling into the sea. Or maybe it’s a beach bar so perfectly placed it feels as much a part of the landscape as the sand. Plenty of beaches are picturesque. These are the ones, if you ask us, that are beautiful.

Industry observers note that barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here. The long stretch of blush-pink sand is framed by low vegetation and blissfully few signs of life. There is, almost puzzlingly, a Nobu, which brings a welcome blip of civilization in the form of Japanese-Peruvian cooking, cocktails, and a beach club with cabanas. (Nobu Beach Inn is set to debut in 2027, too.) Book lunch there and a beach transfer in advance—many of the top resorts on Antigua offer this as a day excursion from the other island.

In a recent development, grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate. An offshore reef keeps the waters agreeably calm for swimming (especially with kids), too. This is one of the Caribbean’s most polished beach destinations, with a concentration of luxury resorts, watersports operators and restaurants that make a choose-your-own adventure beach day a pretty seamless affair. Public access points are plentiful and free, so you needn’t be staying at one of the grand hotels to enjoy the view. (Although you should.).

The kind of place that castaway dreams are made of, Little Bay is a tiny crescent of sand tucked beneath towering limestone cliffs. No beach club, no cabanas, no infrastructure, no fuss. It’s accessible by boat from neighboring Crocus Bay, or, if you’re feeling adventurous, by rope down the rock face. Bring water, a picnic and all your gear—there’s fantastic snorkeling here.

A mile-long horseshoe of white sand with clear, shallow water, Flamenco Beach is more than worth the ferry over from mainland Puerto Rico. It also has an unusual bit of history: two abandoned United States military tanks, left behind after the Navy used Culebra for training exercises, now sit near the shore, covered in colorful graffiti. We aren’t usually proponents of littering, but the counterpoint of natural beauty with human history is part of what makes this beach so unforgettable.

In a recent development, definitely the most photographed beach in the U.S. Virgin Islands and probably the most photographed beach in the Caribbean, Trunk Bay never disappoints. From the access road, you see a sweep of white sand stretching out, with impossibly turquoise waters and a small offshore cay that seems placed for composition. It’s part of Virgin Islands National Park, so the infrastructure covers all the stuff you need—snack bar, restrooms, showers and snorkel rentals. The main attraction is the underwater snorkeling trail, where submerged markers introduce visitors to the coral reef and its inhabitants.

Sources indicate that if you want swanky French beach clubs, head over to Saint-Jean, because Saline is St. Barth’s at its most elemental. The sand is broad and soft, the dunes rolling, and the sea open, with no beach clubs or hotels or influencers interrupting your view. Getting there requires a short walk over the dunes from the parking lot, which helps preserve the feeling that you’re leaving the chi-chi side of the island behind.

According to recent reports, there are beautiful beaches, and then there are the Baths, a landscape so distinctive it feels like you’ve left the Caribbean, and perhaps earth entirely. The beach is home to a collection of enormous granite boulders, some as large as houses, all tumbled together to create something totally unique. Between them are hidden grottoes, tidal pools and narrow passages—making this as much a playground as it is a beach. Bring sturdy water shoes and expect to do some scrambling.

It has been revealed that the longest beach on its island, this elegant crescent sits directly on the Tropic of Cancer. It’s relatively remote and unspoiled by Bahamian standards, making it a true bucket list destination for beach snobs. It’s about a 30-minute drive from George Town on Great Exuma (where the airport is), across the bridge to Little Exuma. There are no proper facilities, so pack what you need. There are Aman, Rosewood and Bulgari resorts debuting here in the years to come—so visit now for serious “I've been coming here since” bragging rights.

It has been revealed that A hidden gem by any standard, Sandy Island is a miniature, uninhabited coral cay located just off the west coast of Carriacou, Grenada’s sister island. There are no hotels or roads, and the whole appeal is the rugged simplicity of arriving by boat, dropping anchor and spending an afternoon doing basically nothing except enjoying the elements. The island is part of a protected marine park, making it a fantastic spot for snorkeling with colorful reef fish, turtles and octopi.

In a recent development, the rest of the world is finally catching up with what the diving scene has known for years—No Name Beach is one of the most pristine, stunning stretches of sand anywhere in the Caribbean. It’s located on the tiny island of Klein Bonaire (“Little Bonaire”) just offshore of mainland Bonaire, and is part of Bonaire National Marine Park, meaning development is off the table. There aren’t any restaurants, bathrooms, or beach bars, but there are water taxis from Kralendijk. Bring food and water, your own snorkel gear, and prepare to be blown away by the untouched Caribbean at its finest.

Industry observers note that while Bávaro Beach proper is about 5 miles long, it connects seamlessly with adjoining beaches Arena Blanca and Arena Gorda—so, depending on who’s counting, actually comes in at closer to 30 miles of uninterrupted shoreline. This is the beach that initially spurred Punta Cana’s resort boom, with coconut palms fringing the white sand, a barrier reef keeping the waters tranquil, and enough space for everyone to stretch out and (pretty much) never feel crowded. If you head toward El Cortecito or Los Corales, you’ll find beach bars where the party never stops. On a beach this beautiful, why would it?

United Airlines CEO Says “The Lead That We Have Is Going To Grow” In Thanksgiving Message To Employees

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby used his Thanksgiving message to thank employees working over the holiday and repeat his conviction that United is the best airline in the world.
  • In a video filmed at San Francisco International Airport and shared with Live And Let’s Fly, Kirby acknowledged the employees who will spend the holiday taking care of travelers rather than celebrating with their own families.
  • He also described hearing regularly from customers about employees who made their journeys easier or did something special for them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby used his Thanksgiving message to thank employees working over the holiday and repeat his conviction that United is the best airline in the world. But his most revealing comment concerned what comes next: he expects United to widen its lead over every other airline.

In a video filmed at San Francisco International Airport and shared with Live And Let’s Fly, Kirby acknowledged the employees who will spend the holiday taking care of travelers rather than celebrating with their own families.

He also described hearing regularly from customers about employees who made their journeys easier or did something special for them. That was the most predictable and customary part of a Thanksgiving message, though Kirby could not resist adding a competitive prediction.

Kirby again called United the best airline in the world, then told employees:.

“I know we’re going to keep that up in the years to come and the lead that we have is going to grow versus all of the other airlines.”.

That is quite a statement, particularly the reference to all other airlines rather than just American or Delta.

Industry observers note that I increasingly enjoy flying United. I recently wrote about how Starlink influences which flights I book, and my experiences with the crews and operation have generally been very positive too. Even as a free agent, I find myself drawn back to United. That is a good position for an airline to be in: winning my business because I like the flight it offers rather than because I need another qualifying dollar toward elite status.

But calling United the best airline in the world remains a much broader claim than I would make. My recent Air France A350 business class flight, for example, offered a level of comfort and dining that United would struggle to match consistently.

It has been revealed that united also still has a wide variation in its onboard product. An A321neo with Starlink and a comfortable cabin presents a very different experience from an older aircraft with unreliable internet.

Industry observers note that we can all understand why Kirby speaks this way to employees. He wants them to take pride in the airline and believe that their work is building something better. But the claim becomes more persuasive when passengers can board any aircraft in the fleet and reasonably expect a similarly good experience. That may be coming, but United is still quite a ways off.

What I appreciated most was Kirby’s emphasis on the individual employees who make travel easier.

Sources indicate that A new cabin or faster internet can influence which flight I book. The way an employee treats me often determines how I feel about that flight afterward and critically to airlines, whether I would recommend it to others (part of the NPS score).

Recent findings suggest that that becomes especially apparent when something goes wrong. A delay is frustrating, but an empathetic employee can preserve a lot of goodwill. Being ignored or brushed aside can turn an ordinary disruption into a reason to book another airline next time, which is a frequent matter for me on American Airlines.

Kirby says customers tell him about those positive encounters, including on the flight he took that day. It also connects with his recent message after the FAA ground stop, when he highlighted a crew helping a mother traveling with three young children. These are the experiences passengers remember, sometimes long after they have forgotten what they ate or which aircraft operated the flight.

Happy Thanksgiving everyone! At United, we’re about connecting people and uniting the world and that’s never more true than over the Thanksgiving holiday when we’re about to have our two busiest days of the travel period. I know many of you are going be working hard at the holidays and missing time with your friends and family so I want to say thank you for doing that and really taking care of our customer during this important time.

According to recent reports, as we enter the Thanksgiving holiday, I’m thankful for an awful lot of things in my personal life but in my professional life, I’m thankful for all that you have done in the last several years to make United Airlines the best airline in the world. I fly a lot, including on my flight today, customers constantly are telling me stories about what a flight attendant or a pilot or a gate agent has done to ease their travel to do something special for them that makes a memory for them. So thank you for all you’ve done in the past several years to vault us to a leadership position.

Industry observers note that thank you for everything you’re doing right now during the holidays to take care of customers and I know we’re going to keep that up in the years to come and the lead that we have is going to grow versus all of the other airlines. Thank you for really doing things to not just make United Airlines the best in the world but to set a newly introduced standard for what it means to be a great airline in global aviation. Happy Thanksgiving and thank you.

Kirby is thankful for the employees who he believes have made United the best airline in the world, and he expects its lead over competitors to grow.

Industry observers note that I share his enthusiasm for much of what United is doing, though I am not ready to award it that title. The more compelling part of his message was the recognition that employees earn customer loyalty through the way they treat people.

According to recent reports, united has given me plenty of reasons to return lately. Continuing to deliver those good experiences will do far more to persuade me than any declaration that it is already the best. To everyone working at the airport or onboard today, thank you. I hope passengers remember that the person helping them get home may be spending the holiday away from their own family.

Breaking: Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1261 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February.
  • Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.
  • According to recent reports, that means staffing up major committees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

According to recent reports, that means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Sources indicate that arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan stated.

Industry observers note that still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she claims of staffers headed there for the first time.

Industry observers note that the work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can promptly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

In a recent development, there’s every indication that pressure will continue in the newly introduced Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, stated Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the upcoming year, if they haven’t already, Melendres remarked.

It has been revealed that “There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he stated.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the upcoming Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a massive part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

In a recent development, lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

In a recent development, for instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Sources indicate that standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Industry observers note that those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, stated he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin noted.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

It has been revealed that U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren noted.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

According to recent reports, “There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”.

It has been revealed that “I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet confirmed — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin remarked.

How a Screen-Free Retreat in South Africa’s Cederberg Rewired My Nervous System

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1491 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as the sun dropped behind craggy peaks, the heat-baked sandstone dissolved into a deep twilight, and the silence thickened until the valley became a dark amphitheater.
  • Recent findings suggest that my phone had lost signal hours earlier, somewhere on the winding, vertiginous drive into this private reserve of over 3,300 acres.
  • Cradled by ancient rock, Weaver’s Nest is a villa for two above the Doring River.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as the sun dropped behind craggy peaks, the heat-baked sandstone dissolved into a deep twilight, and the silence thickened until the valley became a dark amphitheater. I had come to Bliss & Stars, an off-grid retreat perched above the Doring River deep in South Africa's Cederberg, for Orion's Odyssey, a program timed to the new moon, when the sky is at its darkest. As we neared midnight, the Milky Way's galactic core rose above the ridge, so dense and richly textured, it looked like the luminous, flowing reflection of the river below.

Recent findings suggest that my phone had lost signal hours earlier, somewhere on the winding, vertiginous drive into this private reserve of over 3,300 acres. Initially, I had found that confronting, until I made peace with what I stood to gain. The eye needs around 20 minutes of true darkness to adjust, and a single glance at a bright screen largely undoes it. Without a signal, I had no reason to look down at it. It was just a camera.

Cradled by ancient rock, Weaver’s Nest is a villa for two above the Doring River.

That encompassing darkness is what brought Heine Rasmussen, an astronomy and nature guide and science communicator, and his wife Daria, a meditation teacher and somatic practitioner, here. In 2018, they left behind the security of corporate life in Copenhagen for a quest to find the least light-polluted skies. After searching around the world, they found them in the Cederberg, just over four hours north of Cape Town.

They acquired the virtually untouched land in 2019, and first had to construct a rudimentary access road before they could start building the lodge. Everything came in by pickup truck and trailer, and was carried by hand for the last stretch. The chalets were wedged between boulders or into the rock face above the river. More recently, the couple added a villa, bringing the total to six units that can accomodate no more than 10 guests.

On these monthly, stargazing-centered retreats, the nights belong to Heine. After dinner each evening, we gathered on a circular, open-air viewing deck in front of the observatory, where mattresses were laid out so we could lie flat and look straight up. One night Heine led us on what he calls "a little mental space walk," a star meditation designed to unground rather than ground us, during which he recounted the history of the universe. With our eyes closed, we breathed the night in through the nose and out through the mouth while he invited the city's stress to leave with each exhalation, until gravity seemed to loosen its grip and our arms and legs felt as if they might float. Falling asleep, he assured us, was perfectly fine.

After a night of stargazing, morning breathwork and yoga with Daria help put life into perspective.

The Cederberg's sandstone boulders have been sculpted by wind and water over aeons.

At the 20-inch telescope, one of the largest privately owned in South Africa, he taught us without jargon, finding a nebula and talking our small group through it while we took turns peering into the eyepiece. Guests here range from billionaires seeking quiet to people who come for free on the lodge's bursary program, and all of them arrive curious, looking for purpose, or simply to disconnect from the world they’ve left behind.

It has been revealed that heine's first subject: time. Moonlight, he told us, reaches us about a second after leaving the moon; sunlight about eight minutes after leaving the sun. The two pale patches in the southern sky, the Magellanic Clouds, are satellite galaxies of our own, and their light set out more than 160,000 years ago, when our species was young and still almost entirely in Africa. From there he moved to the iron in our blood and the calcium in our bones, forged in stars that exploded before our sun ever existed. I had heard the stardust line many times in other remote locales but never within the context of physics, explained step by step, or woven into a meditation under a sky like this one.

Sources indicate that daria took care of the mornings, which began with a thick, warm ceremonial cacao, readying the nervous system for what was to follow. I missed my regular wake-up coffee, the richness of the chocolatey cacao not compensating for the familiar kick of caffeine. From there, we headed to our yoga mats in an open-air studio where Daria led us in somatic breathwork, referencing the enormity of the night sky. Her view is that star-studded skies like those the Cederberg reliably delivers do not make daily concerns disappear; they merely change their size, put them into perspective. Much of what she imparts during the morning breathwork sessions is about making room to allow yourself to feel that. Daria works with the stress the body becomes so good at absorbing—shallow breaths and a clenched jaw, in my case. From hysterical laughter to sobs of grief, more surfaced for our small circle than any of us had bargained for.

The Cederberg has some of the darkest skies on earth.

After brunch, we hiked narrow paths where Cape mountain leopard tracks were pressed into the sand and raptors like Verreaux's eagles and rock kestrels caught thermals overhead. We scrambled over the orange sandstone rock, carved into fantastical shapes piled like giant, irregular building blocks, before washing off the dust and dry heat in the Doring River, the water surprisingly cool even though it was the end of summer. In the overhangs we marveled at San rock paintings between 2,000 and 5,000 years old, a collection of sites which Heine and Daria are still discovering on their land. There are more than 2,500 known rock art sites in the wider Cederberg, and whenever I see them I can't help thinking that the people who left their mark here once stood in this same silence, under much the same stars.

Every plant-based meal is consciously plated to nourish body, mind, and spirit.

It has been revealed that with so much of the day spent on the move, in silence or alone, meals at the long wooden table in the lodge's open-proposal kitchen became the social high point. With caffeine, refined sugar, meat, and alcohol off the menu, dining still felt indulgent despite being based on vegetables, fruit, and whole grains. Daria has little patience for the guilt and pressure so often associated with clean-eating dogma; in the retreat's cookbook, Eat, Thrive, Repeat, she writes about reaching the point where "appetite becomes information rather than judgment." In practice, that meant buddha bowls, ancient grain salads, roasted vegetables, and sweet treats at brunch like beetroot flapjacks with a miso caramel of dates and coconut oil.

One night, after hiking into the sunset and a surprise dinner in a cave, Heine gave an informal introduction to one of his passions, astrophotography. I learned how to hold a shutter open long enough to gather light the eye cannot. I stood still in the pitch black with a torch under my chin and came away with a portrait of myself against thousands of stars, the camera collecting photons that had been traveling for centuries, some for millennia, before they reached its sensor.

As you fall asleep, the night sky is framed in floor-to-ceiling glass.

Industry observers note that on the final night, the telescope and the table worked in tandem. Dinner with Stars ran to six courses, eaten between turns at the eyepiece, and, read in order, the menu told the life story of the universe much as Heine had been telling it to us since we arrived—from Major Bang, a baked carrot dish, through to The White Dwarf, a wild strawberry dessert named for the small, dense ember a star like our sun leaves behind when it dies. The carbon on my fork was made inside stars that died before our sun existed, scattered into space, swept into the cloud of gas and dust that became our solar system, and pulled from the air, eventually, by the carrots on my plate.

Because it was summer and we had to wait for the sky to turn inky black, nights ended well past midnight. Back in my chalet, on a bed stuffed with horsehair, seaweed, and coconut fiber, I sipped from a flask filled with locally grown rooibos sweetened with wildflower honey before drifting off to sleep. The chalet's floor-to-ceiling windows face east over the river and are free of curtains to encourage waking with the morning light—a gentle but powerful way to reset one's circadian rhythm. When I opened my eyes in the small hours, the night sky filled the glass. I had never seen it framed like that.

Running year-round except July in South Africa's Cederberg, Bliss & Stars hosts intimate, all-inclusive retreats in six off-grid units sleeping a maximum of 10 guests.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the boy grew into a man and his eyes were opened to the world around him, to the beauty of nature, the sights and smells of the world’s great cities, and the elegance of the human race.
  • Industry observers note that humanity, for all its hints of goodness, was inimitably at war with itself.
  • The man took this all in, wondering where his place was in all this was.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the boy grew into a man and his eyes were opened to the world around him, to the beauty of nature, the sights and smells of the world’s great cities, and the elegance of the human race. But he noticed something else, something troubling.

Industry observers note that humanity, for all its hints of goodness, was inimitably at war with itself. Not just wars of weaponry and nation states, but deeper wars of ideas and values. Like a cancer imperfectly treated, the pestilence of irreconcilable division ebbed and flowed…but perpetually manifested itself in fierce battles and spilled blood.

The man took this all in, wondering where his place was in all this was. A humanitarian? A missionary? A soldier? A politician? A writer? A peacemaker? Perhaps a little of each. Perhaps none of the above. He married a woman from a different culture and with a different worldview. The challenge of marriage personified the challenge of the surrounding world — putting differences asides to build trust, loyalty, and respect while growing in love and patience. Was this even possible absent divine intervention?

Sources indicate that then one Thanksgiving Day it hit him. He could not change the world. Not alone anyway. But there was one one thing he could do, something so trite on the one hand but absolutely revolutionary on the other: he could love his neighbor as he loved himself.

Sources indicate that just how would that look? Being honest, generous, forgiving, joyful, peaceful, patient, kind, and faithful to everyone he encountered. He would often fail, but it became a primary goal in life.

According to recent reports, the man still ponders his place in this world, but there is one thing he knows — there may be many things he is not, but he is a traveler and that gives him a unique opportunity to put his maxim to practice in venues far beyond the friendly confines of home. Blessed with so much through circumstance of birth, he pauses to reflect upon the blessings he has been the recipient of, many from those who follow a similar maxim.

Perhaps one day you will meet him and he can encourage you or share in your struggles. His goal is to leave every person he crosses paths with knowing that they are loved and respected. Life is often unkind and this goal is insurmountable in all places and at all times, but it is worth pursuing.

Now, he invites you to join him in his journey to put others before himself. One day and one person at a time, humanity can tame the inhumane world it finds itself in.

This post has appeared annually on Thanksgiving Day since 2015.

A problem with one of Delta’s weight-and-balance systems delayed hundreds of flights Sunday, with backups most acute at the nation’s busiest airport.

According to FlightAware, Delta delayed over 2,100 flights Sunday and canceled 274.

Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport was the hardest hit, with about 700 flights delayed, though not all were Delta connections.

Delta remarked in a statement that its employees were using manual workarounds for baggage processing. It also said it would rebook customers on the next available flight and provide meals and hotel rooms where needed.

The FAA said on X that the problem was specific to Delta and had nothing to do with the agency’s air traffic control system, which crashed on Nov. 13.

Delta is working to resolve problems with the airline’s weight and balance automation system. These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems. Please check with Delta for the latest information. https://t.co/q4Fc59VMYg.

The outage was resolved Sunday afternoon.

As of Monday morning, Delta’s delay rate was down to 6%.

While resolved fairly quickly, the system failure could hardly have come at a worse time. Millions of Americans are flying this week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, and there are concerns that technology outages could again snarl air traffic during the busiest time of the year. The single busiest day for air travel is expected to be Sunday, Nov. 29, after Thanksgiving.

Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that california Rep.
  • Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.
  • Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that california Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, noted House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

In a recent development, working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very matter that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she remarked. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”.

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

“A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”.

Industry observers note that several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he stated.

Industry observers note that the candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez mentioned. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”.

In a recent development, amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto noted.

In a recent development, maybe you’re traveling to enjoy the singular experience of Rockefeller Center and the Rockettes at Christmas time, or you’re a local who’s spending the holidays at home. Regardless, this season is one of the most special times to spend in Latest York City, which makes it an exceptionally busy time of year for restaurants and bars alike.

Even with the foresight to make a reservation or two, it can be a challenge to find a place to enjoy lunch or dinner with a group on Christmas Day; many spots close for the day, while others simply don’t feel quite special enough for a true, Upcoming York City holiday. To help you avoid a last-minute scramble for a table or a less-than-festive dinner date, we’ve curated a guide of some of the very best restaurants open in NYC on Christmas day. Many of these spots will be serving their usual, outstanding menus, while some are offering holiday special cocktails, desserts, and entrées.

Whether you’re looking for a prix fixe meal with reserve wine and spirits selections, or you want to find a spot that’ll fill the younger members of your party with a little holiday cheer, we’ve got you covered.

Industry observers note that known for its Art Deco-inspired design and show-stopping caviar service, the Russian Tea Room is offering a special three-course prix fixe menu for $145 (and $95 for children 12 and under), featuring speciality dishes and restaurant classics. Christmas Day highlights include pan-seared Scallops with roasted butternut squash risotto; apricot-glazed duck with apple, cranberry, Brussels sprouts salad; and a creamy Hojicha-based crème brûlée. Their signature Afternoon Tea service will also be available from 11:30 am to 4:00 pm on Christmas.

Sources indicate that what’s more festive than tucking into a fancy steak dinner on Christmas? Holiday specials at iconic steakhouse Quality Eats include the Après Ski Sangria, featuring red wine, mulling spices and winter citrus; Home Alone, with Angel’s Envy Bourbon, cinnamon and house spruce bitters; and Quality Nog, with Bacardi Ocho, Cognac and homemade spiced nog. Pair any of them with a dry-aged tomahawk ribsteak and 28-Day dry-aged porterhouse served with tableside truffle service.

Sources indicate that if you’re looking for Christmas dinner to enjoy with a group, Limusina’s menu of coastal Mexican-inspired fare is especially shareable; think Serrano Guacamole, Flamed Queso Fundido and a rotating selection of seasonal plates prepared over live fire. The holiday cocktail menu includes the Après Ski Sangria, featuring red wine, mulling spices and winter citrus; Home Alone, with bourbon, cinnamon and house spruce bitters; and Quality Nog, blending Bacardi Ocho, Cognac and a delightful homemade spiced nog.

For Christmas Day, Marcus Samuelsson’s Red Rooster will be serving classic holiday favorites reimagined with a Red Rooster Harlem twist, all with a soulful and spirited celebration filled with music, comfort food, and community. Rooted in the vibrant and inclusive spirit of Harlem, Red Rooster Harlem is inspired by the neighborhood’s African American, Southern, and Caribbean culinary influences with exciting dishes like its signature Yardbird fried chicken, cornbread and gravy, shrimp and grits, oxtail meatloaf, and more.

At Le Crocodile, the cozy French bistro inside Williamsburg’s Wythe Hotel, celebrate Christmas Day with a special prix fixe menu. Dinner starts with hors d’oeuvres like Mushroom Pâté Tarts and Gruyère Cheese Puffs, followed by first-course options such as Beef Consommé with Black Truffle. Roast Beef & Jus and Baked Atlantic Halibut are served family-style with sides including maple-glazed carrots and Brussels sprouts with pancetta. Dessert options include Mont Blanc with Biscoff & Cranberry. Afterwards, head upstairs for a cocktail at Bar Blondeau, and enjoy sweeping views of a (quieter) city.

Recently reopened Koreatown barbecue destination will be open on Christmas Day. It's a luxe alternative to a traditional Christmas setting and a great option for a large group. Menu highlights like the Mother of Pearl Set—with abalone, U10 diver scallops and American wagyu brisket tips grilled at the table—along with the Platter of Nine Delicacies topped with a tin of caviar, will ensure the evening feels appropriately celebratory. Drinks at the downstairs cocktail bar Yangban will begin (or close out) the night on a festive note.

Recent findings suggest that grillhouse and oyster cellar from Sunday Hospitality (the team behind Rule of Thirds, Café Chelsea, Sunday in Brooklyn and more) is open for dinner service on Christmas Day from 2 PM to 8 PM. Located in the heart of Midtown Manhattan, menu highlights include Roast Bone Marrow, a riff on the classic served with housemade barbecue seasoning and a sweet, sticky glaze, Pork Tomahawk with spiced pork jus inspired by jerk flavors, and the famed Dynamo Burger, that can be ordered “drenched” with prime rib au jus served with beef fat fries.

On Christmas Day, enjoy Southern India with specialties like medhu vada (crispy lentil donuts with sambar) and Kerala beef chukka (boneless beef, coconut, shallots, garlic, and spices), along with Sri Lankan favorites like chicken lamprais served in a banana leaf package and kothu roti, a roadside specialty prepared from shredded paratha stir-fried with vegetables, onions, and egg. The beverage program features playful takes on South Indian classics, including the dosa martini, made with Jamun gin, St. Germain, and Lillet Blanc, and the palm paradise (coconut kallu, curry leaves, lychee cordial, and lemon cordial).

Take a trip through Punjab, Goa, Hyderabad, Madras, Calcutta, and Lucknow at Tamarind. For dinner, the menu features nizami keema (ground lamb with cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, and lemon zest), paneer pasanda (fresh cheese in a rich cashew-onion sauce), and Achari Hiran Ki Chhampen (venison chops marinated in hung yogurt, pickling spices, and roasted chickpea flour).

One of the few restaurants in the city open for Christmas lunch as well as dinner, Indian fine dining destination Musaafer is serving up its crowd-favorite paneer tikka, eponymous daal Musaafer, coriander shrimp, and more. The highlight of the menu is a festive plum cake layered with black pepper and Old Monk rum crémeux, cranberry compote, and sudachi lime gelée, topped with delicate makhan malai (milk cream). It’s finished with almond-sugar snowflakes, gold and silver pearls, and a dusting of snow sugar.

Why not ring in the holiday with creations from one of the city’s best pastry chefs? At Lysée, chef Eunji Lee offers a seven-course ($130 per person) dessert tasting menu of savory and sweet pastries; menu highlights include Lysée’s signature Black truffle ice cream cone, made with black truffle ice cream and a slice of chocolate waffle cone and chocolate caramel, a Mont Blanc with cognac ice cream, a mini mushroom quiche, an Ossetra caviar tart, and more. Choose from four two-hour seatings available at 11:30 AM, 1:30 PM, 3:30 PM, and 5:30 PM, with an optional wine pairing.

Storms on Both Coasts Threaten Thanksgiving Travel

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Forecasters are warning that storm systems will likely strike parts of the South, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast, as well as Northern California and the Pacific Northwest.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Powerful storms bringing high winds and the potential for flooding could seriously disrupt commercial air travel in the U.S. during the single busiest week of the year.

Forecasters are warning that storm systems will likely strike parts of the South, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast, as well as Northern California and the Pacific Northwest. These regions are home to some of the nation’s busiest airports, through which millions of American travelers will pass this week en route to visit family and friends for Thanksgiving on Thursday.

Sources indicate that in the Northeast, the remnants of a weakened, disorganized system were still clearing out on Monday. A much stronger storm is expected to develop in the Gulf of Mexico between Monday and Tuesday, impact parts of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic Wednesday, and slam into the Fresh York metro area and New England on Thanksgiving Day.

Industry observers note that according to an advisory from the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center, strong wind gusts up to 50 mph will be felt from the Carolinas to Maine. Flooding and beach erosion could be seen in coastal areas due to the already high tides.

WPC has initiated Key Messages for a Thanksgiving Coastal Storm that is expected to impact the U.S. East Coast. pic.twitter.com/pdQuU4U4yG.

Americans traveling from, through, or to these areas should prepare for the possibility of flooded roads, damage from high winds, and power outages, the agency mentioned.

NYC Emergency Management said Sunday that the storm could bring gusts of 40 to 45 mph and about one to two inches of rain to the city.

For New York and New England, the storm will be at its strongest Thursday evening. Parts of the Adirondacks and northern New England could see ice and snow mixed in with rain.

It has been revealed that in California, Oregon, and Washington, residents still recovering from flooding last week could be hit again by rain and strong winds. A upcoming system is expected to move in Tuesday and Wednesday; combined with the “king tides,” the storm could cause flooding up and down the West Coast.

Industry observers note that the impact is expected to be most severe between Portland, Oregon, and San Francisco. San Francisco’s mayor stated residents should take the forecasts seriously and consider not traveling for the holiday.

The Sierra Nevada, meanwhile, will see fresh snow, meteorologists stated.

According to recent reports, over six million people are expected to fly within the U.S. this week for Thanksgiving. The surge is already underway, with many carriers adding flights to accommodate the increased traffic. American Airlines earlier this month projected its busiest Thanksgiving week since before the COVID-19 pandemic; that prediction could hold true for other U.S. airlines as well.

AirlineGeeks will continue to monitor weather conditions and provide updates as the week progresses.
