Tech Report: Finding Unexpected Kinship With Senior Travelers—And a Joyful Fresh Outlook On Growing Older

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on a grassy field in Don-Aryk, Kyrgyzstan, men on horseback were wrestling over a headless goat carcass.
  • Standing there in the Kyrgyz countryside, being collectively talked out of one of my more impulsive yeses by a busload of surrogate parents, I felt like a teenager being scolded—defiant but also secretly touched that people I had just met cared enough to save me from myself.
  • On my first trip to Uzbekistan, I joined an Intrepid Travel tour and wondered whether I had booked the wrong departure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on a grassy field in Don-Aryk, Kyrgyzstan, men on horseback were wrestling over a headless goat carcass. This is kok boru, the country's national sport, sometimes called dead goat polo. The riders violently wrenched the goat from one another's grip, then tore across the field toward a cauldron-size goal. When the game ended, a player invited me to take a victory lap with the goat. I was two weeks into a Smithsonian Journeys trip across five Central Asian countries with a group of mostly retirees. They knew I was genuinely considering his offer, and their reaction was unanimous: Oh, no you won't.

Standing there in the Kyrgyz countryside, being collectively talked out of one of my more impulsive yeses by a busload of surrogate parents, I felt like a teenager being scolded—defiant but also secretly touched that people I had just met cared enough to save me from myself.

On my first trip to Uzbekistan, I joined an Intrepid Travel tour and wondered whether I had booked the wrong departure. Most of the guests were seniors, so I assumed we would have little in common. Then I met Penny, a septuagenarian from Australia who survived a terrorist bombing in Bali that killed three people in her group. Her husband had suffered brain damage and withdrew from the world; Penny kept traveling, even when it meant going alone. We shopped for textiles in Khiva and bonded over meals; by trip's end, whatever distance I'd imagined between us disappeared.

In a recent development, that first trip changed more than my assumptions about whom I might enjoy traveling with. My own parents struggled with severe depression and agoraphobia, each condition feeding the other as their shared world contracted. Older travelers like Penny indicated me another way to age: by staying curious, social, active, and engaged with the world.

According to recent reports, I saw that same determination on a Lindblad Expeditions–National Geographic cruise through the Peruvian Amazon. Dan and Kathy, both widowed after 30-year marriages, met online, fell in love, and kept a list of trips to take. Another guest had cared for her husband through terminal brain cancer, then received her own cancer diagnosis. Hardship hadn't blunted their zest for adventure; if anything, it had magnified it.

I was on board and turning that contrast over in my mind when I found out my dad died.

The next few days bled together. Through the blur my fellow travelers revealed up for me—listening when I wanted to talk and giving me space when I didn't. These folks knew firsthand what it meant to have life cleaved into Before and After. Yet here they were, swimming with piranhas, trekking through the jungle, and plotting where to go next. They were living proof that joy could still exist on the other side of tragedy.

Back in Central Asia my fellow travelers who had vetoed my kok boru ride embodied what I'd come to love about traveling with groups of older people. Linda, an 80-year-old retired psychoanalyst, shared my raunchy humor and skittering attention span during tedious museum tours. I suspected Susan, 83, disapproved when she first asked about my tattoos—until she rolled up her sleeve to reveal Betty Boop on her biceps, acquired at 81. She had survived two comas and a stroke, and still posed for photos in fire-engine red lipstick. A red lip is my signature too. This was my kind of woman.

The whole group was intimidatingly accomplished: pulmonologists, oncologists, former heads of ICUs and surgical departments. Ask for a doctor, and half the bus could raise a hand. They talked passionately about history and architecture. My PhD dad could turn any conversation into a lecture too; I hadn't realized how much I missed that until I was sermonized at dinner. Their adult children came up often: Would they find the right partner? Start a family? Live up to their potential? Beneath all the second-guessing was enormous tenderness.

Traveling with seniors requires patience, of course. Some use canes and walkers, so itineraries are deliberately less demanding. To me, that's a fair trade.

It has been revealed that on a Viking river cruise that sailed this past summer from Bucharest, Romania, to Budapest, my husband and I hit it off with Bob and Jeannie, a couple from Long Island. They peppered us with questions about our work, our four-year-old son, and our life in Minnesota. That curiosity touched a nerve. My mother, who has dementia and lives with us, no longer asks about my job, my kid, or anything else. Soon we were seeking one another out, talking for hours and doubling over with laughter. We promised to look them up the next time we were in New York—and meant it. Bob and Jeannie weren't filling in for anyone. They were just friends.

At our farewell Smithsonian dinner in Almaty, the group toasted me for “keeping us young.” I was usually the one volunteering to dance with strangers, climb onto horses, or let an owl perch on my head. If I got parental supervision in return, they got to live vicariously through my harebrained antics.

Their gratitude caught me off guard. I knew what these travelers gave me—perspective, attention, a road map for the years ahead—but hadn't considered what I might be giving them.

Recent findings suggest that now, when I join a group trip, I genuinely hope I'm the youngest person on the bus. I look forward to seeing whom I'll connect with, hearing stories I'll carry for years, and, if I'm lucky, getting a glimpse of the person I might become.

    #145779. Latest Update: How to Spend Christmas in Paris

    📅 14 Dec 2017 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2365 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: How to Spend Christmas in Paris

    📅 14 Dec 2017 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2365 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, strasbourg may be France’s holiday capital, claiming the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but there’s no denying Christmas in Paris is a showstopper.
    • Oyster stands are as much a fixture of the holidays in Paris as Christmas markets—which happen to be one of the best places to try them.
    • Read our complete Paris travel guide here, which includes:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, strasbourg may be France’s holiday capital, claiming the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but there’s no denying Christmas in Paris is a showstopper. The city shines brighter each year with thousands of lights illuminating its famous squares and landmarks like the Champs-Elysées, dubbed the “world’s most beautiful avenue.” Holiday cheer seeps into each of the 20 arrondissements, decorated with larger-than-life garlands, forests of bauble-strewn fir trees, sculptural light displays, and wooden chalets doling out vin chaud (mulled wine) and holiday specialties like foie gras—best spread on subtly sweet pain d’épices (gingerbread).

    Oyster stands are as much a fixture of the holidays in Paris as Christmas markets—which happen to be one of the best places to try them. Fête the season in true French fashion with a movable feast dining and drinking at some of the city’s most iconic institutions, from Left Bank cafés where famous writers and artists once gathered to the Palace hotels huddled around Place de la Concorde and Place Vendôme. And when you’re ready to indulge in Paris’s renowned retail therapy, swing by one of the grand magasins (department stores), which rank among the best in the world for their holiday window displays—New York City included—executed with the same style and precision as a couturier. The city may not be blanketed in snow, but the holiday spirit is as strong here as on the slopes in the French Alps—and even has the cuisine and chalets to prove it. If you’re planning to spend Christmas in Paris, you’ll find plenty of ways to celebrate, but these nine are some of the best things to do and see during the holidays in the City of Light.

    Read our complete Paris travel guide here, which includes:.

    According to recent reports, every review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that activity. When choosing things to do, our editors consider landmarks and experiences that offer an insider’s view of a destination, keeping authenticity, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Lindsey Tramuta.

    This winter, Oscar winner Cate Blanchett will lead the lighting ceremony of the 2 million LED lights illuminating the Champs-Elysées, running all the way up to the Arc de Triomphe. Sparkling each evening from 5:00 pm to 1:00 am, the most iconic avenue in Paris and its 400 balloon glass garland-adorned trees are coordinating with another famous landmark—the Eiffel Tower—twinkling in unison on the hour. Every quarter of an hour, the Champs-Elysées will put on a light show set to Vivaldi’s Four Seasons, and on December 24 and 25, the avenue will glow in Christmas-themed green and red. As part of the Upcoming Year’s Eve countdown to midnight under the Arc de Triomphe, when a music-themed fireworks show will ring in 2027, the lights will shine in a tricolor blue, white and red display running down the avenue. Making a grand return after a decade-long pause, a Christmas market will run from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe with more than 200 stalls and an ice rink near the Pavillon Ledoyen.

    Recent findings suggest that dining with a view takes on a whole upcoming meaning as you settle in by the panoramic windows on Ducasse sur Seine, the sole electric boat cruising the river. The floating restaurant is as gastronomic an experience as anything on land thanks to Alain Ducasse, the namesake chef behind the modern Parisian cuisine who claims a record-setting number of coveted Michelin stars. With chef Jean-Philippe Berens and the team prepping everything fresh on board, you’ll have prime views of the Seine while dining in style on Christmas Eve during the six-course menu, which features everything from silky foie gras royale to raw scallops topped with gelée and caviar—plus a cheese course with 18-month-matured truffled Comté.

    Sources indicate that the ambiance is equally as elegant at Ducasse Baccarat, where the chef’s cuisine is presented in an opulent space dripping in chandeliers and tableware designed by the French fine crystal creator. One of the few spots open daily during the holiday season, the restaurant ups the ante on Christmas Eve and Newly introduced Year’s Eve with themed degustation menus.

    It has been revealed that france’s Capital of Christmas, Strasbourg, is home to the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but Paris is dotted with more than a dozen markets and Christmas villages—the largest being La Magie de Noël in the Tuileries Garden, stretching from the Louvre to Place de la Concorde, which remains open until early January. There, you’ll discover hundreds of wooden cabins selling small gifts and seasonal treats; a selection of stands run by French artisans, from glassblowers to woodworkers; and attractions like a small ice rink and carnival rides—the Ferris wheel being the highlight, especially during the Eiffel Tower’s hourly light show.

    Recent findings suggest that on the Square René Viviani, directly across from Notre Dame, you’ll find an intimate market with some 30 exhibitors selling regional food, hot chocolate, and handmade crafts. On the Left Bank, the Saint-Germain-des-Prés Marché de Noël unfolds along the namesake boulevard, next to the church, with wooden chalets and gourmet stands serving up everything from caviar and foie gras to Savoyard favorite tartiflette (a reblochon cheese and potato gratin) and sweet and savory pretzels. Unfolding in the courtyard of the Gare de l’Est train station, the historic starting point for the first Orient Express, the Marché de Noël des Producteurs Alsaciens is dedicated to Alsatian delicacies, with stands displaying regional specialties like kougelhopf, a fluted brioche cake filled with rum-soaked raisins and almonds.

    More than the decorated avenues and elaborate window displays, it is the Bûche de Noël (yule log cakes that may or may not be shaped like logs) that takes the lead as the ultimate holiday essential during Christmas in Paris. While most cakes are prepared and sold for take-away, there are a few spots to linger over tea and an individual slice of the indulgent Christmas cake, including Fouquet’s Paris, where the red, velvety chocolate and roasted corn mousse dessert is designed after the arabesques in the hotel’s historic salons and staircases. At Butterfly Pâtisserie, the Hôtel de Crillon’s boutique and tearoom, pastry chef Matthieu Carlin’s exquisite selection of seasonal pastries, including his Bolivian dark chocolate mousse Bûche de Noël, shaped like a submarine out of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea—a tribute to the hotel’s Jules Verne-inspired holiday theme—can be enjoyed on-site with a cup of tea or a thick hot chocolate, or taken to-go. On the Place de la Concorde, snack on praline hazelnut and pistachio and orange blossom-flavored French toast from the hotel’s garland-strewn, striped winter chalet, or sip espresso martinis at Terrasse Concorde’s pop-up bar, which has been redecorated to mimic the most exclusive of ski resorts with French cashmere house Kujten’s custom-crafted cushions and blankets.

    Sources indicate that at Ritz Paris, craft your own yule log during a baking class, or settle in by the fireplace of the opulent, champagne-colored Salon Marie-Louise for a Christmas tea, where you’ll indulge in spruced-up takes on the afternoon tradition, including truffle cream finger sandwiches, lobster focaccia, and Crêpes Suzettes prepped à la minute. Next door, Ritz Paris Le Comptoir’s carousel-shaped Bûche de Noël has been deemed the city’s most stunning this season—and with only 65 available, it’s a gift unlike any other. Nearby at Mondovi Luxury Suites, chefs come to you for in-suite macaron-making sessions and mixology workshops—and with the “world’s best bartender” Colin Field behind the Le 7 Cocktail Bar, you’ll be learning from the best. On the Left Bank, the palace hotel Mandarin Oriental Lutetia Paris is serving a lavish Sunday brunch buffet, winter-themed afternoon tea with hot chocolate, and pastry chef Nicolas Guercio’s wreath-shaped yule log filled with layers of vanilla mousse, pear confit, and housemade pecan praline.

    Sources indicate that dating back to the mid-13th century, Sainte-Chapelle was once a royal chapel constructed to house the precious Crown of Thorns relic. Today, it’s admired for a different reason: the 15 stained-glass windows—comprised of 1,113 panels—are some of the most impressive in France, let alone all of Europe. Combine sightseeing with an experience only taking place during the holiday season listening to the music of Antonio Vivaldi or Johann Strauss during a classical concert within the chapel’s Gothic nave.

    Paris’s grand magasins (department stores) offer more than retail therapy. Their elaborate holiday window displays executed in couture-like fashion have earned them the title of best in the world—and that even includes Fresh York City. There’s a theme for every taste: The Samaritaine has been designed to feel like you’re taking a Christmas stroll through a snowy Paris, with winter lights and snowflakes crowning the grand magasin’s facade near the Seine. Shop at the indoor Christmas market and rest assured your presents will sit pretty under the tree this year thanks to the help of the pros at the dedicated wrapping studio, who can swath gifts in plush paper and custom-made ribbons. Over at Printemps Haussmann, behind the Opéra Garnier, the department store decorated its windows around the theme of “A Well-Knit Christmas," commissioning artisan-crafted crochet pieces; 160 animated characters (including felt cats and mice) chasing a ball of wool; and costumes by the store’s seamstress, Valérie Cuter.

    In a recent development, at Galeries Lafayette Haussmann, holiday cheer doesn't end at the sidewalk, where French fashion designer Jean-Charles de Castelbajac themed the vibrant window displays around tales of angels and Matisse-inspired shapes. The Christmas tree and holiday displays beneath the store's Art Nouveau dome are an annual event, comparable to Upcoming York City’s Rockefeller Center tree lighting. Always vibrant and impressive, visitors who venture into the atrium of the shop this season will find a tree towering 16 meters high—but this year, the wing-shaped structure follows the animated storybook theme with an angel hovering overhead and a soundtrack by French DJ Vladimir Cauchemar. From the 30-foot-long Glasswalk footbridge, on the third floor of the store, you can catch an even better view of the “tree”—and snap a few photos. Hotels like SO/ Paris, on the banks of the Seine, are also dressing up for the occasion with paper artist Maud Vantours’ sculptural Nutcracker creation, which you can admire while sipping seasonal coffee or an espresso martini along with a slice of the hotel’s Bûche de Noël.

    It has been revealed that nothing warms up locals and visitors like hot chocolate. For the most well-known, head to Angelina on the rue de Rivoli for its thick, decadent Chocolat Chaud Africain that will leave you wondering if they just melted an entire chocolate bar into your cup. If the line snakes around the block, take it à emporter. Near the Opéra Garnier, chocolatier Jade Genin (daughter of legendary Jacques Genin) is famous for her signature Concorde obelisk-shaped chocolate pyramidions, but her modernized take on hot chocolate—entirely plant-based with homemade almond milk—is as much a draw during the holidays. In Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Les Deux Magots’s scarlet banquettes may have been where the literary set like Jean-Paul Sartre once held court, but the cafe is also one of the best on the Left Bank for hot chocolate—where it’s prepared the traditional way, with melted Valrhona blended with warm milk and poured out of a classic carafe.

    While you can spike your hot chocolate with Irish whiskey and Chantilly cream, the city’s leading cocktail bars are taking some of the holiday season’s signature flavors and mixing them into creations like Beurre, Little Red Door’s cocktail version of fresh brioche, with crisp apple, butter, vodka, and yes—bread. At The Cambridge Public House, classic Irish coffee is given a French twist with calvados and silky salted maple cream, while Hôtel Lancaster partnered with historic French tea house Damman Frères for a gingerbread punch blended with rooibos de Noël tea and sherry, served alongside a tonka bean and gingerbread pastry.

    In a recent development, moulin Rouge’s lavish costumes adorned with sequins and rhinestones feel all the more festive when you’re dressed up yourself on Christmas night for a gourmet feast followed by the iconic Féerie revue show. At the Musée des Arts Forains (Fairground Museum), its annual Christmas extravaganza, Le Festival du Merveilleux, runs from December 26, 2026, to January 3, 2027. The makeshift Christmas village transforms into a light-strewn theater with magicians, aerial silk dancers, musicians, puppeteers, and tap dancers putting on dreamlike performances around the Belle Époque funfairs and gardens.

    Recent findings suggest that on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, get your culture fix while sightseeing, sipping champagne, and listening to an orchestra perform carols and violin concertos during a classical Christmas show in one of the world’s most famous landmarks: the Eiffel Tower. And for the full winter wonderland experience, Disneyland Park’s characters are adorned in holiday attire during Christmas parades, musical performances by The Arendelle Carollers in the upcoming World of Frozen, and meet-and-greet moments with Santa hat-clad favorites like Stitch.

    Sources indicate that embrace the festive feel of slope-side specialties like fondue at Chalet des Îles, a historic wooden Swiss chalet reconstructed by Napoleon III for Eugénie that hovers on an island in the Bois de Boulogne. Top Chef contestant and co-founder of Paris’s Ambos restaurant, Pierre Chomet, is behind this season’s fireside feast of Alsatian-style tartes, flambées, and creamy Mont d’Or cheese, while Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme’s timber-clad Chalet du Park has popped up for the season in the Palace hotel’s terrace, serving winter menus designed by Michelin-starred chef Jean-François Rouquette.

    At Hôtel Le Grand Mazarin, join a chocolate expert for small-group tastings, or take a seat for Christmas Eve dinner at candlelit restaurant Boubalé for a Mediterranean take on traditional plates like toasted challah with foie gras and fig and scallops wrapped in kadaif (shredded phyllo) paired with a holiday-themed DJ set. A dinner worth dressing up for, two Michelin-starred Le Clarence, off of the Champs-Elysées, has designed a feast worthy of royalty complete with the finest of ingredients, from dive-caught scallops to lobster and caviar—plus a collector-worthy wine pairing that fêtes the season in true French fashion.

    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.
    • Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

    Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

    “One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries remarked, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

    Industry observers note that the proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

    Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

    Recent findings suggest that “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries remarked. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

    According to recent reports, on healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust latest majority.

    When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

    “Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

    Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

    Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

    Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    Jeffries mentioned Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

    This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

    Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    According to recent reports, the Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    Industry observers note that hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”.

    Sources indicate that “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley noted that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley mentioned. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very tech giant that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox noted in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    “We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson stated. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also remarked that Hawley’s newly introduced arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

    #145772. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1015 w)

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s upcoming ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s upcoming ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., mentioned, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five latest air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it swiftly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    Recent findings suggest that “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, stated Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization strategy so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    Sources indicate that for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., mentioned the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    According to recent reports, “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not significant on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    Recent findings suggest that “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he noted. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    Recent findings suggest that “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy remarked. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    Industry observers note that the telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford stated Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    In a recent development, the decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    How JetBlue's Bag Fee Hike Makes A BlueFirst Base Fare From $249, Bag Included, Look Like A Real Alternative

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that changes are happening at JetBlue Airways.
    • At the same time, JetBlue will soon introduce 'BlueFirst', a domestic first class cabin that will be rolled out fleetwide.
    • JetBlue offers three fare types for its Main, EvenMore, BlueFirst, and Mint cabin classes: Base, Standard, and Flex.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that changes are happening at JetBlue Airways. The airline recently raised its bag fees for economy passengers; as of November 3, the first checked bag will cost between $50 and $70, depending on the day and when the ticket is booked, while a second checked bag ranges from $70 to $85. These are steep prices and noticeably higher than the checked bag fees set by US legacy carriers, while JetBlue's base fares before optional add-ons tend to be lower than the competition.

    At the same time, JetBlue will soon introduce 'BlueFirst', a domestic first class cabin that will be rolled out fleetwide. The carrier will debut this cabin on December 8 on its route from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, before introducing the cabin throughout its network. While JetBlue prices all fares dynamically, BlueFirst one-way fares will start at $249 when the cabin is first introduced, and while this certainly doesn't mean all tickets will be priced this way, those that are will be very compelling compared with the airline's economy cabin.

    JetBlue offers three fare types for its Main, EvenMore, BlueFirst, and Mint cabin classes: Base, Standard, and Flex. None of the fares for Main and EvenMore include checked bags, meaning passengers who want to check their bags need to add at least $50 to the overall price of their tickets. At the same time, the airline's fresh BlueFirst fares do include at least one checked bag, while the BlueFirst Flex fare includes two checked bags. What makes this particularly notable is that BlueFirst fares are actually fairly attractive.

    Recent findings suggest that the airline's one-way BlueFirst fares start at $299 from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, and the route between LaGuardia and Fort Lauderdale follows shortly afterward, with prices starting at $249. Although most tickets are being sold for significantly more, the airline has largely priced BlueFirst fares at about 40% to 70% more than an equivalent Main ticket.

    Recent findings suggest that crucially, however, even the BlueFirst Base ticket includes a checked bag, slightly closing the gap. The BlueFirst Flex includes two checked bags, whereas a Main Flex or an EvenMore Flex fare includes none. While the full cost of a BlueFirst ticket will still be higher, it's closer than expected.

    It has been revealed that with the recent increase in bag fees, BlueFirst tickets do look quite attractive for passengers who will check a bag and are willing to pay more for a better experience. BlueFirst offers a large recliner with added legroom, as well as complimentary meals and premium drinks. It undoubtedly offers a more comfortable experience than Main, and the price difference is not particularly steep once ancillaries are factored. What's more, JetBlue's initial pricing for BlueFirst does not follow the standard practice in the US.

    Generally, the US legacy carriers (which are the airlines that have offered domestic first class the longest) do not price first class tickets at 40% to 70% above economy. Domestic first class fares are usually significantly more expensive than economy tickets, and even when you factor in ancillaries, first class comes at a real price premium. Admittedly, JetBlue's initial BlueFirst tickets are being sold in the competitive Florida market, where fares tend to be low, but they still largely undercut the legacy carriers on price.

    According to recent reports, one way to view this is as a deliberate strategy by JetBlue. The airline has never before offered a domestic first class cabin, and it plans to introduce BlueFirst throughout the network fairly rapidly. Not only do potential customers need to be made aware of the product and exposed to it, but the carrier also needs to pull customers away from American, Delta, and United. Attractive initial fares help with publicity while increasing bookings, which heightens awareness.

    Sources indicate that on the flip side, however, airlines generally charge what they think is the maximum price that customers are willing to pay. JetBlue undercutting competitors on price can also be seen as a reflection of the carrier's pricing power, which isn't a positive sign. One reason JetBlue introduced BlueFirst was to increase revenue, since first class generally commands higher fares. If it continues to undercut competitors on price system-wide, then this would become a problem.

    Recent findings suggest that jetBlue operates like a budget airline, such as Frontier or Allegiant Air. However, the airline has differentiated itself not necessarily through low fares, but through the passenger experience. The carrier offered significantly more legroom in economy, along with seatback screens before they became common on domestic flights. In addition, snack options were diverse, and the airline's later Mint business class on transcontinental and transatlantic routes has been well received.

    Despite its low-cost carrier structure, the airline offers a passenger experience similar to that of legacy carriers, and arguably better in some ways. However, JetBlue has been unable to command a fare premium for its excellent economy product, while its Northeast operations come with high operating costs. In addition, the airline didn't offer first class in the past, further limiting revenue, and the carrier has faced serious challenges expanding its customer base.

    Boston Logan International Airport (BOS).

    Fort Lauderdale Hollywood International Airport (FLL).

    Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    Fresh York John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

    Orlando International Airport (MCO).

    San Juan Luis Munoz Marin International Airport (SJU).

    While JetBlue is an attractive option for customers in the Northeast, its route network is quite minimal outside of the East Coast. Its network and schedules are not attractive to much of the country. In addition, JetBlue has also suffered major reliability challenges. This hurts its appeal to many potential customers, as operational reliability is a major factor in purchasing decisions. While BlueFirst won't solve all of JetBlue's complications, it should help the carrier with its network-wide revenue problem.

    Industry observers note that not only do premium seats such as domestic first class have superior margins to economy seats, but premium demand is through the roof in the US. By not offering a domestic first-class product until now, JetBlue has essentially lost out on lucrative revenue, and several other low-cost carriers are now offering such a product. Frontier and Allegiant Air have both revealed domestic first class cabins to debut in 2027, while Breeze Airways already sells first class seats.

    It has been revealed that notably, JetBlue will largely maintain the same capacity its planes currently have. It will achieve this by cutting seat pitch in Main down to just 30 inches (76.2 centimeters), even though the airline has long been known for offering above-average seat pitch. While this is undoubtedly a drawback for most customers, JetBlue hasn't been able to command a fare premium for offering more legroom. Therefore, it will focus on where the money is, which is in the latest BlueFirst cabin, while it will also make its cabins more space-efficient.

    Of course, BlueFirst won't solve all of JetBlue's issues; the airline has limited national relevance, and on-time operations remain challenging. What's more, JetBlue's overall financial situation has deteriorated significantly over the past several years. However, the new BlueFirst cabin should help the airline's revenue stream and also make the airline more appealing to potential customers, who may have stayed away from the airline due to the lack of a domestic first class cabin.

    In a recent development, for travelers living in Latest York, Boston, Florida, or San Juan, JetBlue offers fairly comprehensive schedules and good route options. However, airlines such as Delta Air Lines and United Airlines operate routes that span the entire country, making them relevant nationally. In addition, these airlines have long offered domestic first class, which is a major reason to be loyal to one airline. What's more, JetBlue's operational reliability issues make customers more hesitant to choose it over other airlines.

    According to recent reports, the airline has not made money since 2019 and has posted a $257 million loss for the third quarter of 2026. The carrier has attractive assets, including a large slot portfolio at Newly introduced York JFK Airport, and is generally liked by its loyal customers. However, the route network loses money, and frequent-flyer engagement is not high enough to offset these losses (legacy carriers make most of their money through co-branded credit card engagement rather than ticket sales).

    Industry observers note that the carrier has been implementing the 'JetForward' turnaround plan to cut unprofitable routes, improve operational reliability, and refocus on leisure customers. BlueFirst is one of the most consequential decisions the airline has made in recent years, and it should significantly improve the carrier's revenue stream given strong demand for premium cabins today. What remains to be seen is whether the JetForward initiative and moves such as introducing BlueFirst will be enough to ensure the airline's long-term survival.

    Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1425 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that senate Minority Leader Charles E.
    • Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a fresh majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec.
    • That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a fresh majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

    That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

    The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

    In a recent development, but supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

    “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

    Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

    “And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

    Several senators leaving the meeting mentioned the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

    That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

    With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

    It has been revealed that “No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., stated Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

    It has been revealed that “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

    Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the upcoming people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

    “They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she stated.

    Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday mentioned at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

    “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

    Sources indicate that but there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

    Sources indicate that “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., remarked Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the upcoming ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

    Industry observers note that several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

    Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

    That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who mentioned he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

    It has been revealed that kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

    Sources indicate that “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

    In a recent development, “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he stated. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

    In a recent development, sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

    “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he stated. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

    Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for newly introduced leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

    It has been revealed that senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

    “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan stated.

    Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

    “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

    “That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

    In a recent development, sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

    Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

    “I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

    Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    United Airlines Pilot Suspended On TSA Orders Over Support For Terror Group, Report Says

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) has reportedly directed United Airlines to suspend a pilot last week over alleged support for a terrorist organization.
    • The reported intervention follows several controversies surrounding United pilots and comes amid heightened international scrutiny of aviation personnel following an attempted terrorist attack aboard a flydubai flight in September.
    • According to recent reports, the federal intervention reportedly occurred between November 16 and 22, and included the withdrawal of the pilot's Known Crewmember (KCM) credential, which facilitates expedited security screening for eligible airline employees.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) has reportedly directed United Airlines to suspend a pilot last week over alleged support for a terrorist organization. According to a report by Jewish News Syndicate (JNS), citing a federal government source, the pilot's crew security credential was also revoked. Neither the pilot's identity nor the terrorist organization they allegedly supported has been disclosed.

    The reported intervention follows several controversies surrounding United pilots and comes amid heightened international scrutiny of aviation personnel following an attempted terrorist attack aboard a flydubai flight in September. CNN reports that US security agencies have subsequently issued a joint advisory to the aviation industry warning of renewed calls for attacks against commercial aviation.

    According to recent reports, the federal intervention reportedly occurred between November 16 and 22, and included the withdrawal of the pilot's Known Crewmember (KCM) credential, which facilitates expedited security screening for eligible airline employees. The existing program is already undergoing significant changes, with the Association of Flight Attendants confirming that its replacement, the Crewmember Access Point (CMAP) program, will be administered directly by the TSA by the end of 2026.

    The suspension follows earlier reporting by journalist Mike Wagenheim on November 17, citing two sources who alleged that United was aware of up to six additional crew members who had expressed support for terrorist organizations. According to View From The Wing, the federal source subsequently alleged that resistance from the pilots' union contributed to the TSA's decision to intervene.

    JNS approached both United and the TSA for comment on multiple occasions, but was not able to obtain a response from either organization. However, Michael Wilson, spokesperson for United's Master Executive Council of the Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA), explained that the union assesses allegations against its professional ethics code and United's workplace guidelines, stating that:.

    “[The union] has a robust professional standards committee and legal team that evaluates any accusation or pilot action.”.

    The latest case follows renewed scrutiny of United Captain Ibrahim Mossallam, a Newark-based pilot qualified to operate the Boeing 757 and 767. United initially suspended Mossallam with pay in November 2023 after he published social media comments praising the October 7 Hamas-led attacks on Israel. According to Airline Ratings, he subsequently returned to flying duties, although Aerotime reported last month that United had confirmed that he had again been removed from service pending a review.

    A separate controversy emerged in October when the Jerusalem Post reported that Israeli authorities had barred United pilot Sina Amjadian from operating flights into the country following allegations of support for Hezbollah and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). However, United responded that Amjadian, a Boeing 737 pilot, was not qualified on United's long-haul aircraft, and had been on leave since 2024.

    Mossallam publishes controversial comments concerning the October 7 attacks.

    United suspends Mossallam with pay.

    Mossallam reportedly returns to flying duties.

    Amjadian begins a leave of absence.

    United confirms Mossallam has again been withheld from service.

    United denies reports of Mossallam's immediate reinstatement.

    Israel's restrictions on Amjadian become public.

    Allegations emerge concerning six additional crew members.

    TSA reportedly orders the suspension of an unnamed pilot.

    Details of the reported TSA intervention are published.

    While United has confirmed the employment status of both previously identified pilots, several other allegations remain unverified. The carrier has also explicitly denied reports that Mossallam returned to flying immediately after his latest suspension. Nevertheless, the reported intervention by federal authorities raises important questions about where an airline's responsibility for assessing potential security threats ends, and the government's begins.

    Recent findings suggest that the potential consequences of insider threats were demonstrated on September 30, when a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv became the subject of an attempted terrorist attack involving its first officer. The aircraft landed safely in Saudi Arabia, and the UAE's attorney general subsequently characterized the incident as an attempted suicide attack.

    In the US, the TSA's authority extends considerably beyond airport security checkpoints. Under Section 46111 of Title 49 of the US Code, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) must take action when notified by the TSA of a qualifying security threat. The TSA can also request that the action take immediate effect and, separately, concern mandatory security directives to airlines.

    Prevents flying for that employer.

    Withdrawal of crew security privileges.

    Removes expedited crew access privileges.

    Requires airlines to implement specified security measures.

    Temporarily removes relevant flying privileges.

    Removes privileges conferred by the certificate.

    Although there is no evidence that the United pilots were planning similar attacks, the broader security threat remains real. On November 19, the FBI, Department of Homeland Security and TSA jointly warned US airlines and airports about extremist calls for further attacks following the flydubai incident. While authorities were reportedly unaware of any specific credible plot, the advisory underscores the importance of preventative security measures, rigorous personnel vetting, and federal intervention powers.

    Bermudian flag carrier BermudAir will nearly double its U.S. footprint next year as it rolls out latest connections across North and Central America and the Caribbean.

    The carrier announced Tuesday that it will serve Fresh Orleans; Nashville, Tennessee; New Haven, Connecticut; Burlington, Vermont; Portland, Maine; San Antonio; New Brunswick, Canada; Ocho Rios, Jamaica; San Salvador, El Salvador; and San Pedro Sula, Honduras, for the first time.

    BermudAir at the moment serves eight U.S. cities, all on or close to the East Coast, and three destinations in Canada. Its main hub is L.F. Wade International Airport in St. George’s, Bermuda.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thepointsguy ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Yet another giant upcoming cruise ship takes to the sea

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The cruise world welcomed another giant on Wednesday as MSC Cruises took delivery of one of its largest ships ever, the 216,638-ton MSC World Asia.
    • Built at the massive Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France, the 20-deck-high, Asia-themed vessel is the third in the line's latest World Class series of ships — by far the biggest ships that MSC Cruises has ever built.
    • Perhaps more notably, it is the tenth largest cruise ship ever built by any line, smaller only than Royal Caribbean's three Icon Class ships and six Oasis Class ships.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The cruise world welcomed another giant on Wednesday as MSC Cruises took delivery of one of its largest ships ever, the 216,638-ton MSC World Asia.

    Built at the massive Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France, the 20-deck-high, Asia-themed vessel is the third in the line's latest World Class series of ships — by far the biggest ships that MSC Cruises has ever built.

    Perhaps more notably, it is the tenth largest cruise ship ever built by any line, smaller only than Royal Caribbean's three Icon Class ships and six Oasis Class ships.

    "Our ambition is simple: To give every guest the best holiday ever," MSC Group executive chairman Pierfrancesco Vago said Wednesday during a dockside ceremony at the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard to mark the vessel's official handover to MSC Cruises.

    MSC Group is the parent company of MSC Cruises and sister brand Explora Journeys, a luxury line.

    "We invested in rethinking spaces, developing newly introduced concepts and reshaping the experience," Vago added during remarks from a stage set up just in front of the MSC World Asia's bow.

    Vago noted that 60% of the spaces on MSC World Asia are either upcoming or significantly redesigned as compared to the two World Class ships already sailing, MSC World Europa and MSC World America.

    Like those two vessels, MSC World Asia has nearly 2,600 rooms and is capable of holding a whopping 6,758 passengers with every berth filled — more than almost any other passenger vessel afloat.

    It also has similarly massive dimensions with a length of 1,093 feet — the equivalent of nearly four football fields stacked end-to-end — and a width of 154 feet.

    But many of its interior and exterior venues, including a sprawling decktop water park with multiple waterslides and a record-setting dry slide that drops 11 decks, are different from what you'll find on the earlier World Class ships in ways significant and small.

    Related: The terrifying, record-breaking slide on MSC World Asia.

    Among the most significant changes is the addition of upcoming dining and food concepts, including MSC Cruises' first pan-Asian restaurant and a Venchi chocolate and gelato venue.

    Like the earlier World Class vessels, the ship also offers a sushi bar, teppanyaki restaurant, American-style steakhouse and a branch of the Italian chain Eataly (presently found only on MSC World America), among 20 dining options in all.

    In addition to the water park and dry slide, MSC World Asia's top decks offer multiple pool areas; a suspended-over-the-ocean swing ride called The Cliffhangar; and a ropes course.

    According to recent reports, notable interior features include a three-deck-high dining and entertainment zone called the World Galleria, which is covered by one of the largest LED-lit ceilings at sea. An outdoor extension of this area, called the World Promenade, features more dining and entertainment, plus a newly introduced suspended, illuminated Dragon sculpture — part of the ship's Asia theming.

    Related: MSC Cruises cabins and suites guide.

    The arrival of MSC World Asia marks the latest milestone in MSC Cruises' rapid expansion.

    With the addition of MSC World Asia, the brand now operates 24 ships, up from just 13 vessels as recently as 2017. It has nine more on order.

    According to recent reports, the ships on the way include five more World Class vessels scheduled for delivery by 2031. Also coming is a upcoming class of four somewhat smaller, 180,000-ton vessels that will be known as the Frontier Class.

    Wednesday's delivery ceremony included a ceremonial lowering of the Chantiers de l'Atlantique and French flags in front of attendees and the raising of the MSC Cruises flag as well as the flag of Malta, where the vessel is registered.

    MSC Group chief financial officer Alexa Aponte Vago, who is married to MSC Group executive chairman Pierfrancesco Vago, served as the traditional "godmother" for the event, which included the smashing of a bottle of Champagne against the ship's hull.

    Joining her husband on stage, Alexa Aponte Vago cut a ceremonial blue ribbon to release the bottle of Champagne against the side of the vessel right on the letter C in its name.

    In a recent development, while it included a bottle smash, Wednesday's event was not the vessel's official naming. That will take place Saturday in Le Havre, France, at a much larger event.

    MSC World Asia will then head to the Mediterranean, where it will begin its first cruises with paying passengers on Dec. 4 with a voyage out of Barcelona.

    The ship initially will operate seven-night Mediterranean voyages that include stops in France, Italy, Malta and Spain.

    Recent findings suggest that in November 2027, it will reposition to the Southern Caribbean for seven- to 14-night sailings. The itineraries will include stops in Saint Lucia, Grenada, St. Maarten, Antigua and Barbuda, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

    #145762. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (765 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov.
    • Industry observers note that former Rep.
    • The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

    Industry observers note that former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

    The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

    With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

    “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

    The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

    Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

    According to recent reports, she entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

    She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

    But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The Newly introduced York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

    Peltola has noted she had no connection to the scheme.

    It has been revealed that prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

    Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

    The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

    But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

    "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

    According to recent reports, in other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

    The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.
