    #145761. Why A Part 103 Ultralight Needs No Pilot's License In The US & Weighs Under 254 Pounds

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1550 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why A Part 103 Ultralight Needs No Pilot's License In The US & Weighs Under 254 Pounds

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology.
    • He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair.
    • A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

    He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

    A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

    According to recent reports, many people assume that flying any type of aircraft requires extensive training, a pilot certificate, medical approval, and federal registration. While that holds true for most types of licenses, such as a Certified Flight Instructor certificate (CFI) or Airline Transport Pilot (ATP), the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has long maintained a narrow exception that allows certain recreational flyers to take to the skies without obtaining a pilot license. The exception falls under FAA Part 103, a section of federal regulations governing ultralight vehicles and the strict limitations placed upon them.

    While Part 103 is broadly described as allowing someone to fly without a license, the reality is more nuanced. The regulation applies only to a highly specific category of lightweight recreational aircraft that must meet strict performance, weight, and operating requirements. Understanding what qualifies under Part 103 helps explain where the FAA draws the line between recreational freedom and traditional pilot certification requirements.

    Yes, you can legally fly an aircraft in the United States without a pilot certificate, but only if the aircraft qualifies as an ultralight vehicle under FAA Part 103. These vehicles occupy a unique regulatory category that exempts operators from requirements including pilot licensing, aircraft registration, airworthiness certification, and medical certification. The exemption was created to support recreational flying while limiting risk through strict aircraft performance restrictions.

    For powered ultralights, the FAA limits empty weight to 254 lb (115.2 kg), fuel capacity to five gallons (18.9 liters), maximum level-flight speed to 55 knots, and maximum power-off stall speed to 24 knots. Because these aircraft are intentionally small and limited in capability, the FAA regulates them differently than conventional airplanes.

    In a recent development, the concept dates back decades, when regulators sought a framework that would allow simple recreational flying without imposing the full regulatory burden associated with general aviation aircraft. Rather than focusing on pilot certification, Part 103 controls risk by limiting what the aircraft can do. According to the FAA's regulations, qualifying ultralight vehicles are intended solely for sport and recreational purposes and are limited to carrying a single occupant.

    A common misconception is that any small aircraft can be flown without a license. In reality, FAA Part 103 sets detailed technical requirements an aircraft must meet to qualify as an ultralight vehicle. The term Ultralight is a specific category issued by the FAA for licensing and certification, such as airplane, rotorcraft, or glider for pilot ratings. While an FAA certificate typically prints the category and class, the lack of a true license requirement omits this display.

    It has been revealed that the most important requirements involve weight, occupancy, fuel capacity, and performance. Powered Ultralights operate on the basis of minimal configurations of these variables. Ultralight aircraft should not be confused with Light Sport Aircraft, the next category up in the FAA's classification; they also have slightly different regulatory requirements, such as a higher speed limit of 250 knots and the ability to carry an additional passenger. These privileges come at the cost of training for a sport pilot certificate, among other requirements as outlined in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart J, and 14 CFR Part 91.327.

    Maximum 5 gallons (18.9 liters).

    Recent findings suggest that unpowered ultralights, such as many hang gliders, fall under a different weight limit. Under Part 103, these vehicles must weigh less than 155 pounds (70.3 kg) empty. By restricting both weight and performance, the FAA effectively prevents Part 103 aircraft from evolving into conventional airplanes that would normally require certification and pilot qualification.

    Although operators are exempt from licensing requirements, they are not exempt from federal aviation regulations. FAA Part 103 establishes operational limitations designed to protect both ultralight pilots and the public on the ground. Interestingly enough, Ultralight aircraft are not governed by either 14 CFR Part 61 or Part 91, which is the usual home for general aviation operation guidelines.

    Among the most notable restrictions are where and when ultralights may fly. Operations are generally limited to daylight hours and must avoid congested areas, cities, towns, and open-air assemblies of people. The rules also restrict operations within controlled airspace (Class A, B, C, D, E, and most special use airspace) unless prior authorization has been obtained from air traffic control.

    These requirements show that the FAA's approach is not deregulation but targeted regulation. Operators may not need a pilot certificate, but they are still responsible for understanding airspace, weather conditions, and applicable operating restrictions before every flight. For many ultralight enthusiasts, voluntary training remains a common safety practice despite the absence of a licensing requirement.

    While FAA regulations do not require formal flight training for Part 103 operations, aviation organizations consistently encourage it. Groups such as the Experimental Aircraft Association (EAA) have long promoted structured training programs for ultralight pilots, emphasizing that regulatory exemptions do not eliminate the risks associated with flight.

    The EAA's Ultralight Sourcebook notes that Part 103 provides significant operational freedom but also places responsibility squarely on the operator. Similarly, many flight instructors and aviation educators recommend dual instruction in two-seat trainers before attempting solo ultralight operations. Pilot Institute has also highlighted that, despite the absence of licensing requirements, knowledge of weather, aerodynamics, and operating limitations remains critical for safe flight. Industry recommendations reflect a broader understanding that flying skills and regulatory requirements are not necessarily the same thing. A pilot may legally operate a Part 103 vehicle without a certificate, but aviation organizations generally view training as one of the most effective safety measures available.

    Cost is another notable variable. While flight training for a Private Pilot License (PPL) can range from $9,000 to $130,000, Ultralight aircraft operation has a less burdensome barrier to entry. Because no official license is required by the FAA, training costs alone are significantly lower. In general, however, ultralight aircraft are much less common in the general aviation landscape than, for instance, a Cessna 172. The good news is that outright ownership of ultralight aircraft is also more accessible. Aerocorner reports that the cheapest new ultralight aircraft in 2026 is the Mini-Max 1103R, a single-seat wood-and-fabric kit that Mini-Max USA lists at $10,899.99 for the airframe. Also available is a finished, ready-to-fly example at about $22,500.

    Sources indicate that the same restrictions that make Part 103 accessible can also limit its practicality. Ultralight aircraft operation is the strictest modality of aviation under the FAA's jurisdiction. While the qualifications are generally among the most accessible to the public, that accessibility comes with significant compromises. Aircraft designed to remain under the FAA's weight and performance limits generally offer less range, lower speed, and reduced capability compared to certified airplanes.

    Weather sensitivity is another consideration. Because ultralights are lightweight and often have minimal protection from the elements, operating conditions that might be manageable for larger aircraft can present greater challenges. The single-seat requirement also prevents pilots from carrying passengers or instructors during normal operations. Under Part 103, ultralight vehicles must fly during daytime hours with visual reference to the surface and meet basic Visual Flight Rules (VFR) weather minimums for their prescribed airspace. Reference to published manufacturer minimums is also imperative, particularly with respect to wind.

    Recent findings suggest that prospective ultralight pilots should also remember that local airspace considerations still matter. Before operating any Part 103 vehicle, operators should ensure they understand applicable airspace restrictions and any authorization requirements that may apply near busy airports. In the United States, ultralight aircraft cannot fly over congested areas or crowds, and they cannot enter controlled airspace (Class A, B, C, D, or surface Class E) without prior Air Traffic Control (ATC) authorization. Advisory Circular AC-91-36D also suggests that ultralight pilots voluntarily remain above 2000 feet (609.6 meters) above ground level (AGL) wherever possible.

    The short answer is yes: FAA Part 103 allows certain ultralight vehicles to be flown legally in the United States without a pilot certificate, aircraft registration, medical certification, or airworthiness approval. However, that freedom exists only because the FAA imposes strict restrictions on aircraft weight, speed, fuel capacity, occupancy, and operating conditions.

    Recent findings suggest that rather than creating a loophole in aviation regulation, Part 103 represents a carefully structured compromise. The FAA permits recreational flyers to avoid many traditional certification requirements while ensuring that the aircraft themselves remain limited in capability and risk exposure.

    For aviation enthusiasts, Part 103 continues to provide one of the most accessible entry points into personal flight. Yet the regulation's enduring message remains clear: while a license may not be required, safe operation still depends on knowledge, preparation, and respect for the limitations of both the aircraft and the environment in which it flies.

    According to recent reports, more than 417,000 flights will operate in the U.S. this week and early next week as Americans travel ahead of and after Thanksgiving, according to the FAA.

    If accurate, that figure would translate to the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years.

    Tuesday is expected to be the single busiest day of the interval, with more than 52,000 flights.

    In a recent development, air traffic will dip only slightly on Wednesday (49,831 flights) and nearly halve on Thanksgiving Day (27,619 flights) itself, the FAA remarked, with a rebound following Friday to Tuesday, Dec. 1. There will be over 50,000 flights per day on the Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday after Thanksgiving.

    Perhaps aiming to assuage concerns from the public after a turbulent couple of weeks, transportation officials said they are prioritizing traveler safety and taking “unprecedented action” to limit flight delays and cancellations.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted that the Trump administration has assembled a “tiger team” of experts to prevent another mass ground stop.

    Industry observers note that “Our air traffic controllers and safety professionals are working around the clock to keep Americans moving during what is expected to be the busiest Thanksgiving travel week in 16 years,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford mentioned in a statement. “The growing demand for air travel makes it more important than ever to continue modernizing our air traffic control system and build a national airspace system for the 21st century.”.

    Sources indicate that the FAA is also advising travelers to get to the airport early and check with their airline for updates if bad weather seems likely to impact their trip. The agency noted the high likelihood of thunderstorms in the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast this week.

    • Sources indicate that qantas is currently set to launch five new routes between January and October 2027.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that qantas is currently set to launch five new routes between January and October 2027. They include a new link announced on November 26, when this article was written, which will be operated by QantasLink. Of course, compared to some of the other entries, it might not seem particularly noteworthy, but it is in its own right.

    As the article only focuses on 2027, the upcoming link from Sydney to Las Vegas, which will begin on December 29, is not included. Qantas will serve this market six times weekly using the Boeing 787-9. It'll be the first time that scheduled flights have existed, although charter services operated in the past.

    Obviously, a lot of the attention is on the much-discussed nonstop service from Sydney to London Heathrow, which will deploy the Airbus A350-1000ULR. The maximum block time is expected to be around 21 hours.

    Reflecting the highly prestigious nature of the route, AeroRoutes indicates that it'll use QF1/QF2, which is currently on Qantas' one-stop operation from Sydney to Heathrow via Singapore. The stopping service will then use QF5/QF6. Those numbers are currently on Sydney-Perth-Rome, which will become QF105/QF106.

    3 weekly QantasLink Dash 8-Q400 (Sunstate). See the next section.

    According to recent reports, 4 weekly QantasLink E190 (Alliance). Jetstar also operates.

    Sources indicate that 4 weekly QantasLink E190 (Alliance). Jetstar also operates.

    Industry observers note that 3 weekly 787-9. Qantas will now have 3 routes to South Africa. It'll be Cape Town's longest nonstop service in the Southern Hemisphere.

    The so-called Project Sunrise, and everything related to it, has been discussed in detail on many occasions. Tickets are meant to go on sale in February.

    According to recent reports, theoretically, the nonstop operation to Heathrow will cover 9,100+ nautical miles (16,853+ km) each way. However, this is before adjusting the distance because of detours for closed airspace and chasing tailwinds and lower airspace costs. It'll cover more distance than that. Still, even before the alteration, it'd exceed the length of what is presently number one, Singapore Airlines to Upcoming York JFK, by around 11%.

    In a recent development, questions might be raised about the appeal of the upcoming nonstop service from Albury to the popular Gold Coast, which will have a maximum block time of two hours and 20 minutes on the Q400. However, QantasLink will be the third airline to attempt it since 2017.

    It has been revealed that cirium Diio data demonstrates that the now-defunct JetGo flew in 2017/2018 using the Embraer ERJ135 and ERJ140. The now-defunct carrier Bonza followed in 2023/2024 using the Boeing 737 MAX 8. Bonza primarily focused on unserved markets, whether without head-to-head competition or brand-latest.

    Recent findings suggest that like low-cost carriers elsewhere, Bonza used its higher-capacity equipment with much lower seat-mile costs to offer much more attractive fares, compounded by flying nonstop rather than connecting on the way. The lower fares were entirely to drive demand and therefore to grow the market's traffic.

    Booking data shows that Albury-Gold Coast passengers increased by nearly 400% to over 23,000 in a year after the airline's entry. Of course, demand stimulation from the lower fares depressed the yields, but that always happens with LCCs. It is unclear if Bonza's fares fell by more or less than the traffic growth. It is unknown what the average fare was to achieve an approximate 80% load factor.

    Recent findings suggest that qantasLink's operation will be radically different. It'll deploy the 76-seat Q400 rather than the 189-seat MAX 8, reducing round-trip weekly seats for sale from 1,134 to just 456. It'll not have to discount anywhere near as dramatically. That's just as well, as its much higher costs wouldn't let it, at least not sustainably. That's why its minimum round-trip fare is about USD$344 (AU$518). By only flying at more popular times of the year, rather than for weeks at a time and having to discount more, yields will not be depressed.

    QantasLink's new route to the Gold Coast will cover 579 nautical miles (1,072 km) each way. However, if statute miles are used instead, it'll be 666 miles, the so-called number of the beast. Schedule analysis suggests that only 11 routes globally will have this great circle distance when the Q400 service lifts off in March.

    It will be Albury's second-longest turboprop-driven scheduled link in nearly three years. QantasLink had operated the Q400 to Brisbane between July 2021 and May 2024, but that route has switched to the 96-seat E190 (other capacities operate occasionally). More seats contributed to the route's frequency falling to daily, down from the record high of two daily flights with the Q400.

    #145754. Breaking: How Many Lockheed C-5 Galaxies Are Left In 2026?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1614 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: How Many Lockheed C-5 Galaxies Are Left In 2026?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Lockheed C-5M Super Galaxy is the largest military transport aircraft built for the United States Air Force and the third largest in the world (after the now-destroyed Antonov An-225 and the An-124).
    • The US Air Force is the only C-5M operator, and it now aims to keep the type flying far longer than it once expected.
    • The C-5 Galaxy traces its roots back to 1961, when the US Air Force started looking for a heavy jet-powered aircraft to replace its Douglas C-133 Cargomasters, while also complementing its Lockheed C-141 Starlifters.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Lockheed C-5M Super Galaxy is the largest military transport aircraft built for the United States Air Force and the third largest in the world (after the now-destroyed Antonov An-225 and the An-124). A total of 52 Super Galaxies remain active, with the rest in storage, scrapped, written off, or cannibalized for parts. Most flying C-5Ms are upgraded C-5Bs, although there are also some upgraded C-5As.

    The US Air Force is the only C-5M operator, and it now aims to keep the type flying far longer than it once expected. Its Fiscal Year 2027 budget request moves the fleet's retirement to FY2050, five years later than the previous plan, even though only about 37% of the jets were mission capable in FY2025. Here is how many C-5s were built, what happened to them, and how many still exist.

    The C-5 Galaxy traces its roots back to 1961, when the US Air Force started looking for a heavy jet-powered aircraft to replace its Douglas C-133 Cargomasters, while also complementing its Lockheed C-141 Starlifters. The US Army also wanted the Air Force to procure a strategic airlifter larger than the Starlifter, able to carry outsized loads. By 1964, the project had led to the 'Heavy Logistics System' program and received proposals from the US's then-existing airplane makers.

    In a recent development, the companies in question were Boeing, Douglas, General Dynamics, Lockheed, and Martin Marietta, and their proposals came with engine options provided by General Electric, Curtiss-Wright, and Pratt & Whitney. The Air Force selected the Lockheed design with General Electric's TF39 engines (the first high-bypass turbofan to enter service). The USAF liked the Boeing design but rejected it, and Boeing took elements of it to develop the Boeing 747-100 with Pratt & Whitney engines.

    A total of 131 Lockheed C-5 Galaxies were produced, of which 81 were C-5As. In the 1970s, these were found to have cracks in the wings, forcing the Air Force to drastically reduce allowed payloads until fresh strengthened wings were installed on 77 remaining C-5As between 1981 and 1987.

    Industry observers note that the Lockheed C-5 Galaxy has been a pivotal air mobility asset for the United States Air Force for decades. It is responsible for the rapid deployment of combat forces to any point in the world at short notice. First delivered in 1970, the Air Force explains that, "the C-5 has seen extensive use in every major global contingency since the Southeast Asia War.".

    Industry observers note that the massive airlifter provides range and cargo capacity that greatly exceed the capabilities of the airlifters that came before it. Not only do these aircraft transport soldiers, smaller aircraft, helicopters (including three CH-47 Chinooks), armored vehicles, munitions, and supplies, but they can also accommodate two Minuteman Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles. A standard crew is seven: two pilots, two flight engineers, and three loadmasters (see how many crew members it takes to fly a C-5 Galaxy).

    Lockheed C-5M Super Galaxy specifications (per the US Air Force).

    4,800 nautical miles with 120,000 pounds of cargo (7,000 nautical miles with no cargo).

    4x General Electric F138-GE-100 engines.

    It has been revealed that one notable operation for the Galaxies came on October 14, 1973. On that day, the C-5s flew the first Operation Nickel Grass mission to resupply Israeli forces during the Yom Kippur War. Operation Nickel Grass saw the United States supply Israel with 22,325 tons of supplies, including tanks, artillery, and ammunition, using C-141 Starlifters and C-5 Galaxies.

    In a recent development, as stated, Lockheed delivered a total of 81 C-5A variant aircraft, as well as producing the improved C-5B variant. Two C-5As were upgraded to the C-5C standard to carry larger cargo, like satellites. Lockheed proposed the improved re-engined C-5D in the 1990s as an alternative to the McDonnell Douglas C-17 Globemaster III strategic airlifter, and, while this didn't happen, design elements of the C-5D were later used for the C-5M Super Galaxy program.

    Lockheed planned to produce a civilian variant of the Galaxy, called the L-500. The organization developed a design for both passenger and cargo versions of the aircraft, with the passenger aircraft being able to carry up to 1,000 passengers (far more than an Airbus A380). While the designs attracted some interest, in the end, no airlines purchased the aircraft, and it wasn't produced.

    In the late 1990s, it was found that 80% of the Galaxy's airframe service life was still remaining, so the USAF embarked on upgrading 52 examples with GE CF6 (General Electric F138-GE-100) engines, the same family of engines that power the Boeing 767. These produced 22% more thrust, provided a 30% shorter takeoff roll, and other improvements. Other aspects, like avionics, were also upgraded. The Air Force received its first upgraded C-5M in 2008, with work concluding in 2018.

    Recent findings suggest that of the 131 Galaxies produced, Planespotters.net lists six as having been written off. One (66-8303) was damaged beyond repair after a ground fire during maintenance in one of its 12 fuel cells, and another (67-0172) was destroyed by a fire that broke out in the cargo compartment while taxiing. 68-0218 crashed while attempting an emergency landing amid 'Operation Babylift,' where it would have taken Vietnamese orphans to the US as South Vietnam collapsed and the Fall of Saigon neared.

    According to recent reports, planespotters.net lists 15 C-5s as scrapped, with another example listed as 'partially scrapped.' These are all older C-5A models built from 1969 to 1972. A further 37 are stored, mostly at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona, while one is listed as 'preserved.' That airframe (69-0014) is on display at the Air Mobility Command Museum at Dover Air Force Base. 70-0451 was meant to be displayed at the Travis Air Force Base Heritage Center, but was scrapped after space couldn't be found.

    Fate of the USAF's Lockheed C-5 Galaxies.

    According to recent reports, multiple sources confirm that a total of 52 C-5 Galaxies are listed as active. All of these have been upgraded to the C-5M Super Galaxy standard and are newer airframes, with most of them having been built between 1985 and 1989 and originally delivered as examples of the C-5B Galaxy model. The Air Force now looks to keep them in service until FY2050.

    It has been revealed that the Air Force's FY2027 budget request pushes the C-5M's retirement back to FY2050, The War Zone reported. Earlier intends had the fleet bowing out around 2045. The jets are also getting harder to keep serviceable: about 37% of the fleet was mission capable in FY2025, down from 49% the year before.

    Their replacement is still more than a decade away. The Air Force expects the first aircraft from its Next-Generation Airlift (NGAL) program around 2038, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine, and each NGAL aircraft is set to replace one C-5M until the last Super Galaxy retires. The same program is expected to succeed the C-17 eventually, which is why the Air Force believes one aircraft can replace both.

    Sources indicate that according to AMARC Experience, the boneyard at Davis–Monthan Air Force Base has a total of 57 Lockheed C-5A Galaxies in storage, well above the 37 stored airframes Planespotters.net lists. While these airframes exist, it is unclear how many have been mothballed in a condition where they could feasibly be reactivated and returned to service, and how many are just being cannibalized for spare parts. The 309th Aerospace Maintenance and Regeneration Group has different 'Type' categories for its aircraft stored at the boneyard.

    Type 1000 aircraft are placed in long-term storage and are maintained until recalled to active service. These are aircraft that have a high potential to return to flying status, and parts are not permitted to be removed from them. They are 're-preserved' every four years. Meanwhile, Type 1500 includes aircraft that were previously fully preserved, and Type 2000 includes aircraft whose parts are available for reclamation. These are cannibalized.

    Type 3000 includes aircraft on 'flying hold,' where aircraft are kept in flyable condition in short-term, temporary storage as they are transferred elsewhere. Type 4000 aircraft are in excess of US military needs and may be broken down for scrap, recycled, or have their usable parts reclaimed. It is unclear how the Galaxies at the boneyard are classified, but it is possible that some are Type 2000 and others are Type 1000.

    Recent findings suggest that production of the C-5 Galaxy ended in 1989, while production of the C-17 Globemaster III ended in 2015, and there is now no discussion of putting the C-5 back into production. However, there is chatter at Boeing (which absorbed McDonnell Douglas) to restart production of the comparatively diminutive C-17. The chances of the Globemaster going back into production are unlikely, but if it does, it would likely be for export orders.

    Recent findings suggest that few strategic military transports remain in production today. None are in production in the United States, while the smaller Airbus A400M Atlas strategic/tactical airlifter is being produced in Europe, and Russia is producing the Ilyushin Il-76 airlifter in low numbers. The Il-76 is sized between the A400M and the Globemaster. China has also put its Xi'an Y-20 airlifter, which resembles the C-17, into production.

    With no new C-5s coming, 52 remain in service. Add the stored airframes and the preserved example at Dover, and somewhere between 90 and 110 C-5s still exist, depending on whether you take Planespotters.net's storage count (37) or AMARC Experience's (57). The C-5M is still the Air Force's largest airlifter, although large aircraft are increasingly seen as vulnerable, and the Air Force is looking for more roles to be taken over by smaller S/VTOL aircraft where possible.

    • After close to a year of dire financial warnings, Norway’s Norse Atlantic Airways mentioned Wednesday that its situation is “critical” and that it must obtain short-term financing to continue operations.
    • It has been revealed that the Arendal-based carrier has struggled with higher jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
    • According to recent reports, “[The firm’s financial condition is] dependent on securing financing to meet its short term liquidity needs and to continue its operations,” officials remarked in a statement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After close to a year of dire financial warnings, Norway’s Norse Atlantic Airways mentioned Wednesday that its situation is “critical” and that it must obtain short-term financing to continue operations.

    It has been revealed that the Arendal-based carrier has struggled with higher jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In the months since the war started, the airline has cut staff, furloughed some crew members, suspended unprofitable routes, and instituted temporary pay reductions for some non-flying crew, but these steps have apparently not put Norse Atlantic back on solid ground.

    According to recent reports, “[The firm’s financial condition is] dependent on securing financing to meet its short term liquidity needs and to continue its operations,” officials remarked in a statement. “Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover.”.

    Industry observers note that “Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution,” the message continued. “Norse will provide further information as and when appropriate.”.

    It has been revealed that rising fuel costs have set back airlines around the world, but the squeeze is arguably worst in Europe, since the continent depends mainly on Gulf oil and has little domestic refining capacity. The crisis has forced Latvia’s airBaltic into bankruptcy, teed up EasyJet’s sale to Apollo Global Management, and inflicted considerable damage on Lufthansa’s core brand.

    It was not immediately clear if Norse Atlantic has any candidates in mind for a potential merger. The carrier is not part of any global airline alliance, though it partners with operators such as EasyJet, Norwegian Air Shuttle, and Pegasus through its Norse Connections program.

    Bloomberg reported in 2023 and 2024 that the carrier was weighing alliances with larger airlines, possibly through an equity stake, but none were named.

    Norse Atlantic operates only long-haul flights. Its network has been adjusted multiple times over the last year in an effort to reduce costs.

    Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority.
    • Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S.
    • According to recent reports, the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

    According to recent reports, the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

    The latest office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

    Britt, R-Ala., noted the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

    “This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting latest technologies and gaps between sectors,” she noted in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”.

    The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

    It has been revealed that the office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

    Industry observers note that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

    The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

    In a recent development, the House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

    Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring.

    It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

    “If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide noted.

    #145751. Why Flight Attendants Sit Facing Backward During Takeoff & Landing

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1496 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Flight Attendants Sit Facing Backward During Takeoff & Landing

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1496 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Have you ever noticed that flight attendants sit facing backward during take-off and landing?
    • The jumpseat is a very crucial part of an aircraft's safety equipment and is designed to protect the crew members during taxiing, takeoff, and landing, which are critical phases of flight when accidents are more likely to occur.
    • In a recent development, flight attendants face backward in their jump seats during takeoff and landing primarily for safety.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Have you ever noticed that flight attendants sit facing backward during take-off and landing? While most passenger seats are forward-facing, some business-class configurations have rearward-facing seats, which some passengers dislike; therefore, backward-facing seats are rarely used for passengers.

    The jumpseat is a very crucial part of an aircraft's safety equipment and is designed to protect the crew members during taxiing, takeoff, and landing, which are critical phases of flight when accidents are more likely to occur. It is important that the crew are protected at these times so that they can evacuate the aircraft if necessary.

    In a recent development, flight attendants face backward in their jump seats during takeoff and landing primarily for safety. During a sudden stop or impact, a rear-facing seat backrest absorbs the force across the back, shoulders, and head instead of concentrating it on a strap across the chest, as in a car. The seatback supports the head, neck, and torso during sudden forward deceleration, reducing strain on the spine and neck and improving force distribution.

    Sources indicate that rearward-facing seats are safer for the upper torso and reduce the impact on the body in landings or emergencies. Crew seats facing backward are designed to allow brace positions during normal or abnormal takeoff and landing and help protect against debris. That is why infants are encouraged to stay in backward-facing car seats for as long as possible. During sudden deceleration, your body naturally wants to keep moving forward.

    The jumpseat protects the crew from severe injury and helps them stay conscious and mobile in an accident, so that they can direct an evacuation and assist passengers in an emergency. They are always positioned near the emergency exits so that they can respond swiftly. In the event of an accident, cabin crew are better protected than passengers in forward-facing seats. The crew member needs to be conscious and uninjured in an emergency for a fast, efficient evacuation and to potentially save lives.

    It has been revealed that cabin crew jumpseats are almost always facing rearwards. While most face backward toward the tail, some jumpseats face forward or sideways depending on the aircraft type, cabin layout, and door position. They can be single or double jumpseats. Double jumpseats are usually found in the aircraft galleys at the main doors, while single jumpseats are often next to emergency exits throughout the cabin. On private jets, jumpseats are commonly forward- or side-facing depending on type, although they differ from those on commercial jets and may have a different harness and no safety equipment underneath.

    Forward- or sideways-facing seats still meet certification rules and use multipoint harnesses and brace positions to protect the crew. The seat base flips up when the crew member stands, so it doesn’t block the exit during an evacuation. The seats are heavily padded around the back and head area and are next to or inside the galley and adjacent to exit doors. A four-point safety harness secures the crew member firmly during take-off and landing. The lap belt must sit low and tight across the pelvis (not the stomach), with shoulder straps snug and free of twists. It has a single release point.

    According to recent reports, below each standard crew jumpseat, there is a container that holds the life vest, a torch, and a manual release tool for the oxygen system. An interphone is attached to every seat or double seat for communication with the crew and flight deck. Around the seat and above the seat, there will be a smoke hood, fire gloves, and a fire extinguisher. During the emergency equipment check, crew must ensure the harness is fully functional and fitted correctly.

    According to recent reports, facing into the cabin allows crew members to observe the passengers and spot hazards during critical phases of flight. It also ensures passengers follow safety instructions and are seated when the seat belt sign is on. They can typically be used only by airline crew, depending on the airline's policy. There are more jumpseats than the minimum working crew onboard. There are also jumpseats in the flight deck, but there are very strict rules on who can use them.

    In a recent development, these seats are strategically located so that the flight attendants have visibility over different areas of the cabin on take-off, landing and whilst taxiing. There is also the potential to spot unruly passengers or if someone is sick and needs help. They also need to prepare for the silent review in case of evacuation and observe outside conditions through the windows to prepare as needed.

    It has been revealed that however, in the rear or aft galley, this would not be the case as the passengers cannot be seen clearly if the cabin crew are in their harnesses. On some aircraft types, such as the Airbus A320, one cabin crew seat in the aft is stored flat but maneuvered to face forward, and an extra crew member can observe the rear cabin from there if carried.

    While rear-facing seats offer strong impact protection, airlines generally keep passenger seats forward-facing due to passenger preference, motion sickness concerns, and structural or weight factors. Aircraft burn more fuel due to heavy rear-facing seats, making them less popular with airlines.

    Sources indicate that there is also some psychology behind them. Passengers don’t want someone facing opposite them as a rule, as it makes them feel uncomfortable. Some people don't like the sensation of flying backwards, and it could cause motion sickness in some people. It could also be an issue in an evacuation knowing which way to go, as passengers tend to head in the same direction as the door where they entered the aircraft.

    In a recent development, although backward-facing seats are more commonly found in military aircraft, some airlines offer seats that face backward. If you do want to try out a rear-facing airplane seat, opt for business class seats with airlines like American Airlines, United Airlines, Qatar Airways, and British Airways. The brace position for passengers in rearward-facing seats is different from that of the standard brace position.

    The cabin crew brace position is specifically designed to prevent the body flailing, protect limbs needed for opening emergency exits, and minimize head and neck injuries during an impact. When facing the back of the aircraft, impact forces push the body backward into the seat. The back and head should be firmly against the seatback and headrest to prevent whiplash. Knees are together, and feet are placed flat forward or back depending on the airline and whether facing forward or rearward.

    It has been revealed that hands should be placed under the thighs with palms facing up or down, depending on airline procedures, or may be placed on the knees and elbows tucked in to avoid fractures. If facing forward, the chin should be placed down towards the chest and feet slightly forward. In an abnormal landing, the brace position is the same apart from placing hands one on top of the other behind the head with elbows brought together in front of the face and not covering ears, so commands can still be heard. This may differ at different airlines.

    It has been revealed that where there is a side-facing jumpseat, feet should be flat on the floor, hands should be tucked under thighs or placed on the knees. However, extra support is needed, and the head and body should lean against the adjacent bulkhead or headrest on the side toward the direction of impact, securing the shoulder harness tightly.

    Crew adopt a "semi-brace" or standard brace posture during every normal takeoff and landing. This is often paired with a "silent review" of emergency exit procedures, so they are protected against sudden runway excursions or aborted takeoffs and prepared for any incident or accident. They secure themselves in their jumpseats on the flight crew's command: "Cabin crew seats for take-off" or "Cabin crew seats for landing.".

    On most narrowbody aircraft, both the forward double jumpseat and rear double jumpseat face rearward, apart from the Airbus A320, which has another seat at the rear that faces forward into the cabin. On widebody aircraft, seats can be single at some exits, and the double seats in the rear galley may face forward depending on aircraft type.

    In a recent development, in the United States, 14 CFR 25.785(h) claims a flight attendant seat must be “near a required floor-level emergency exit”, that one must sit adjacent to each Type A or Type B exit, and that the rest must be “evenly distributed among the required floor-level emergency exits to the extent feasible”. The rule requires a flight attendant seat to be forward- or rearward-facing with an energy-absorbing rest supporting the arms, shoulders, head and spine, and to sit near a floor-level emergency exit. The brace position differs depending on which way the seat faces and the airline's safety procedures.

    Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M.
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.
    • Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no declared opponent, won decisively, 251-11.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

    Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no declared opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

    “It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries stated at a press conference following the election.

    While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

    In a recent development, “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get substantial things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”.

    Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

    “Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these problems,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”.

    Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

    “This is the beginning of a fresh bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

    Sources indicate that rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

    Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

    At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

    “We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

    “I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”.

    Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

    In a recent development, pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

    Jeffries mentioned Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”.

    Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

    He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

    “House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

    #145747. Why 97% Of Boeing 777 Pilots Continue An Unstable Approach Instead Of Going Around

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1551 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why 97% Of Boeing 777 Pilots Continue An Unstable Approach Instead Of Going Around

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that boeing 777 pilots, like their counterparts on the vast majority of aircraft at most airlines, have set-in-stone parameters they should work within prior to carrying out landings.
    • But most of the time, flight crews push on with a landing even if the criteria for a stable approach are not met.
    • Sources indicate that whether an approach is stable or not is essentially based on the carriers’ own standard operating procedures (SOPs) being met before a minimum height is reached during descent.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that boeing 777 pilots, like their counterparts on the vast majority of aircraft at most airlines, have set-in-stone parameters they should work within prior to carrying out landings. These ensure what is known as a stable approach and give pilots a clear set of rules to stick to when committing to a landing. If they are not met, the decision should be easy: go around and try again.

    But most of the time, flight crews push on with a landing even if the criteria for a stable approach are not met. Thankfully, this does not mean the majority of landings are made in such conditions. However, it leaves a huge disparity between what should be done and what is actually done when it comes to almost all unstable approaches. Why? Well, psychology and the human factor play a huge part in what is really a very short space of time relative to an overall flight.

    Sources indicate that whether an approach is stable or not is essentially based on the carriers’ own standard operating procedures (SOPs) being met before a minimum height is reached during descent. That is according to the Flight Safety Foundation (FSF), which coined the term “stabilized approach” in its Approach and Landing Accident Reduction (ALAR) toolkit back in 1998. In this, the organization recommended a minimum height of either 1,000 feet (305 meters) or 500 feet (152 meters) above airport elevation in instrument or visual meteorological conditions (IMC or VMC), respectively.

    According to recent reports, the FSF’s recommendations stretched to specific criteria behind a stable approach. Simply put, these suggested the correct flight path, speed, landing configuration, and rate of descent by 500 feet (152 meters) in good weather, leaving only small control tweaks needed. Some leeway was granted, namely around speed and sink rate. Overall, though, there was a clear-as-day checklist there for airlines and flight crew alike.

    FSF stabilized approach criteria in VMC, from Sky Library.

    The aircraft is on the correct flight path.

    The airspeed is not more than the reference landing speed (VREF) plus 20 knots (23 mph / 37 kmh) indicated speed, and not less than VREF.

    The aircraft is in the correct landing configuration.

    Sink rate is no greater than 1,000 feet (305 meters) per minute.

    Power setting is appropriate for the aircraft configuration and is not below the minimum power for the approach as defined by the operating manual.

    All briefings and checklists have been conducted.

    All of this aimed to further ensure safety at what is realistically the most dangerous part of a flight. Indeed, the FSF’s toolkit came after its own research found that unstabilized approaches were a causal factor in 66% of 76 accidents and serious incidents during the final stages of those flights between 1984 and 1997. Through the guidance, the organization sought to aid airlines and pilots in preventing aircraft from arriving at runway thresholds too high, too fast, out of alignment, incorrectly configured, or otherwise unprepared for landing.

    It has been revealed that the issue is that the recommendations appeared not to give the industry the overwhelming push the FSF would have desired. Almost two decades after the organization published the toolkit, it cited evidence that indicated almost all unstable approaches were still resulting in aircraft touching down in another report.

    Sources indicate that some 95% to 97% of flight crews whose aircraft were in an unstable state continued to touch down, its 2017 report into go-around decision-making stated. This problem of go-around policy non-compliance, the FSF went on to conclude, was “real” and “arguably the largest threat to flight safety” presently. Improving compliance would be “significant,” it added.

    Recent findings suggest that among a string of findings that the report laid out, it noted the industry had “predominantly” turned to reducing unstable approaches, rather than incorporating go-arounds as standard practice, to avoid accidents in the final stages of flights. But clearly, entirely eradicating unstable approaches was always going to be impossible. When it came to why pilots still pressed on despite finding themselves in such situations, the reasons were plentiful.

    It is easy to pass judgment from the outside. Pilots are tasked with safely delivering passengers, and so what seems an overwhelming disregard of parameters put in place to minimize the risk of incidents raises some pretty serious questions. It is important to consider the realities in cockpits, though, in order to paint a picture of why unstable approaches may be ignored. Among the most blatant factors is timing.

    Sources indicate that take the 777 from Boeing, which is among the bestselling widebody series ever produced. If traveling long-haul frequently, there is a good chance you will have stepped foot aboard a 777 variant at some point. Pilots behind the controls of a 777 have well under a minute of decision-making time after reaching the vital 500 feet (305 meter) threshold at which an approach should be stable. At an appropriate landing speed of 132 knots (152 mph or 244 km/h), a typical 777 will touch down 35 to 42 seconds after hitting this point.

    Recent findings suggest that boeing itself recommends approach speeds for different 777 variants of between 139 knots (160 mph or 257 km/h) and 150 knots (172 mph or 278 km/h), so this could vary. Either way, the point stands: A pilot might have little over half a minute, while in the thick of bringing an aircraft down safely, to process whether a go-around is required, make that call, and then carry it out. That is not to try and justify landings made following unstable approaches, but the timing factor does offer some useful context.

    It is really in the context of timing that the human factors behind landings made after unstable approaches start to make sense. The FSF remarked in 2017: non-compliance with go-around policies was the “industry norm”; awareness of risks among pilots and management was “low”; policy itself was viewed as “unrealistic”; and the practice of going around came with its own complexities and caveats. All of this meant pilots could well have had such thoughts racing through their minds when deciding what to do with an unstable approach.

    It has been revealed that pilot James Albright provided an insight into the decision-making process in such circumstances previously. “If 95% to 97% of flight crews are failing to go around when their SOPs tell them to, we have a problem with the crews, the SOPs, or both,” he wrote. “Too many of us find ourselves in unstable approaches and believe, ‘I can save this.’ The fact that we almost always do reinforces our decision to deviate from our stable approach rules.”.

    But there could be other factors at play, Albright noted in the particular account of a landing made despite questions surrounding the stability of the approach. Among them was the fear that other crew members may not be supportive of a decision to go around, passengers might complain, or questions might be asked by employers. Naturally, that lingering thought of what a delay might entail is worth bearing in mind.

    Arguably, the key reason most unstable approaches result in landings is down to how go-arounds are viewed. Whether it be fears that the maneuver is riskier than a landing, lack of training, or the belief that go-arounds are only for exceptional cases, potential misconceptions frequently pop up as reasons why they might be avoided.

    Guidance from the International Air Transport Association (IATA) stated in 2026: “It is the responsibility of operators to develop and promulgate a clear policy on go-arounds.” Such policy, the trade body stated, should state that a go-around was “a normal flight maneuver” and something “to be initiated whenever a continued approach would not be safe” or, notably, “when the approach does not meet the stabilized approach criteria”.

    But the body went a step further, noting operators should clarify that there would be “no punitive response from management to a go-around” and any failure to do so “when appropriate” would be followed up. All of that goes to say, questions looked to still be there among pilots over when to go around, and how that decision may be received.

    While perhaps somewhat alarming to those unfamiliar with being behind the controls of an aircraft, the important thing to remember is that most landings do indeed follow stable approaches. As the Flight Safety Foundation reported previously, 95% to 97% of all unstable approaches were continued to landing. However, just 3.5% to 4% of all approaches were unstable. So, before vowing never to set foot on a plane again, rest assured that the majority of landings are carried out following approaches that meet SOPs.

    It has been revealed that what these figures do mean is that there is room for improvement across the industry. Whatever the psychological factors preventing pilots from going around in most cases, the practice is yet to be normalized. With that, fears around the likes of causing delays, judgment from colleagues, or carrying out a go-around need to be addressed. As the FSF wrote in 2017: “No other single decision can have such an impact in the reduction of aviation accidents as the decision to go around.”.

    Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1211 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, president Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov.
    • Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.
    • Recent findings suggest that trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, president Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images).

    Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

    Recent findings suggest that trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

    The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

    Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, stated Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one glitch with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

    It has been revealed that “As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

    Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”.

    Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., noted part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

    “They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” remarked Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

    That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

    “I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump stated Monday. “I think he's backing down.”.

    Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a significant reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

    Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, stated Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”.

    “I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”.

    During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

    “Enforcement of the upcoming rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat stated, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

    Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

    “Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”.

    But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

    In a recent development, he stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

    Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, stated Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”.

    It has been revealed that trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the manufacturer’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

    Sources indicate that the administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”.

    Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”.

    It has been revealed that “Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear challenges dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”.

    #145744. Industry News: FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (890 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.
    • Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

    Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

    The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

    In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

    “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”.

    It has been revealed that thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

    Cruz stated at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”.

    “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz remarked. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”.

    Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing.

    The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

    “The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they noted.

    They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about prepares for such an inquiry.

    Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

    In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

    “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter noted.

    On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

    “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related challenges,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

    Industry observers note that democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

    Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

    “I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján remarked, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”.

    Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., remarked at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”.

    In a recent development, “I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

    Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.
