    #145742. Breaking: Why Airline Joint Ventures Are Accused Of Keeping Transatlantic Fares High

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1663 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Why Airline Joint Ventures Are Accused Of Keeping Transatlantic Fares High

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Three antitrust-immunized joint ventures now dominate transatlantic aviation: United Airlines with Lufthansa and its Star Alliance partners, Delta Air Lines with Air France-KLM and Virgin Atlantic, and American Airlines with British Airways and Iberia.
    • Sources indicate that the underlying accusation is more precise: partners who share revenue and set fares together stop competing on the nonstop routes where their networks overlap.
    • Recent findings suggest that an alliance alone does not permit pricing coordination, since carriers in an arm’s-length codeshare each set their own prices, with the operating airline keeping the revenue and the marketing partner collecting a booking fee.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Three antitrust-immunized joint ventures now dominate transatlantic aviation: United Airlines with Lufthansa and its Star Alliance partners, Delta Air Lines with Air France-KLM and Virgin Atlantic, and American Airlines with British Airways and Iberia. A Wendover Productions video, as summarized by Pulse, claims they control roughly 75% of New York to Europe flights and labels them cartels, a framing that belongs to the video rather than to regulators.

    Sources indicate that the underlying accusation is more precise: partners who share revenue and set fares together stop competing on the nonstop routes where their networks overlap. Defenders say the same coordination lowers prices for most travelers who connect. Both claims have empirical support, and evidence from the Department of Justice and a study commissioned by the Department of Transportation shows where each holds, where it weakens, and why the argument has persisted for years.

    Recent findings suggest that an alliance alone does not permit pricing coordination, since carriers in an arm’s-length codeshare each set their own prices, with the operating airline keeping the revenue and the marketing partner collecting a booking fee. Antitrust immunity changes that arrangement by allowing partners to decide fares, schedules, and other competitively sensitive matters jointly across the routes included in their agreement.

    In a recent development, the joint ventures go further by pooling revenue, as partners in a metal-neutral structure share ticket revenue on covered routes under a capacity-based formula, leaving them indifferent about which airline flies a given passenger. A study for the Department of Transportation described the result as carriers behaving like a single airline on the routes in question. American, British Airways, and Iberia argued in 2009 that this removes the incentive to keep a partner’s nonstop flight out of the other carrier’s reach, because a customer choosing it would otherwise transfer revenue away from the selling carrier.

    Joint ventures exist partly because ownership rules in the United States and European Union preclude cross-border mergers, making revenue-sharing agreements the closest available substitute for a single airline. DOT approves them under a public interest standard that can weigh foreign policy goals. The video adds that the pooled partners publish matching prices on overlapping flights, citing United and Brussels Airlines selling the same 6:00 PM Brussels departure at the same fare, which it presents as evidence of price fixing.

    It has been revealed that in a 2011 discussion paper, Antitrust Division economists William Gillespie and Oliver Richard analyzed fares from 2005 to 2010 on 115 routes linking the 20 largest cities in the United States and the European Union. They counted immunized partners serving the same route as a single competitor and found that average one-way fares were $31 higher on routes with one independent nonstop competitor than on routes with two, $62 higher than with three, and $88 higher than with four.

    According to recent reports, those gaps equal roughly 7% of the average fare for each competitor lost, and each was statistically significant at the 99% confidence level. The authors read the result as consistent with the ordinary antitrust presumption that reducing competition raises prices, and they observed that nonstop fares averaged 8.3% above connecting fares, yet most economy passengers on the sampled routes still chose nonstop service.

    It has been revealed that the paper also documents how concentrated the market has become, since three immunized groups, one in each alliance, carried more than 82% of US-EU passenger traffic in the year ending June 2009, and by late 2010 more than half of the sampled routes had a single independent nonstop competitor. Because foreign-carrier fares for itineraries without a US carrier are not public, the economists treated US-carrier fares as representative, a limitation that qualifies any reading of the data. The authors stressed that the paper reflects their own views rather than an official Justice Department position.

    Defenders of the structure rely on double marginalization, the idea that when two unaffiliated carriers price their own legs of a connecting trip, each ignores how its markup reduces demand for the other, so the combined fare ends up too high. Partners that share revenue internalize that effect, which should lower fares for itineraries that require both carriers.

    Sources indicate that A study by economists Jan Brueckner and Ethan Singer, performed under contract to the Department of Transportation and released in 2019, tested the idea on fares from 1997 to 2016. It found that joint venture itineraries were priced about 7.2% below interline tickets, and that their fares were statistically indistinguishable from those of single-carrier trips. On transatlantic routes, the joint venture discount reached roughly 9% across cabins.

    The Justice Department paper offered a rebuttal rather than a denial, since its economists agreed that alliances reduce connecting fares relative to interline tickets yet found that within SkyTeam and Star Alliance, immunized itineraries were no cheaper than non-immunized alliance itineraries, implying the pricing benefit does not require immunity. In the 2019 study, alliance partners without immunity priced just 0.7% below interline tickets, compared with 6.4% for immunized partners, which supports the claim that immunity matters. The two bodies of work therefore agree that connecting fares fall under alliances and disagree mainly on whether immunity is what makes them fall. The Justice Department economists added that 68% of US-EU passengers connected in 2009 across all itineraries, which is why the efficiency claim matters even though nonstop routes carry the higher fares.

    According to recent reports, the same Transportation Department study also found evidence that critics cite, reporting that in the later years of its 1997-2016 sample, granting immunity or joint venture status to two previously unaligned carriers on an overlapping route was equivalent to removing a competitor, with fares rising accordingly. The effect appeared in economy class, where an additional immunized or joint venture pair raised fares by about four to 13% depending on the specification, while business class fares indicated no such overlap effect. That finding is notable because most earlier studies had found no nonstop effect, a point the authors flag as unusual.

    In a recent development, the authors nonetheless concluded that alliances are beneficial on balance, based on a simulation of removing two joint ventures. On one route, nonstop passengers would save about $2.1 million a quarter while connecting passengers would pay about $3.1 million more; on another route, nonstop passengers would save roughly $469,000, while connecting travelers would pay about $10.8 million more. Brueckner and Singer also noted that the exercise ignores convenience gains such as single check-in and shorter layovers, which would further favor alliances.

    It has been revealed that several cautions apply: the simulation covers two unnamed routes, the study pools regions, and the authors call removing a single joint venture unrealistic because it would affect other routes. Studies using structural models, which the authors cite, found no evidence of collusion on nonstop fares, so the literature remains divided on whether partners truly price together.

    Critics argue that the harm persists because newly introduced competitors struggle to enter the overlapping routes. Slot scarcity at hubs such as Heathrow, where the video states slots sell for tens of millions, makes an incumbent partnership’s capacity hard to challenge. DOT has sometimes required remedies, including the divestiture of four Heathrow slots by the oneworld applicants, before granting immunity in 2010. The Justice Department economists also noted that applicants offered few specifics on new service, observing that American launched Dallas/Fort Worth to Madrid more than a year before receiving immunity.

    Recent findings suggest that carve-outs, which bar partners from coordinating fares on specific overlapping routes, have a weaker record. DOT excluded routes such as Frankfurt to Chicago from United and Lufthansa’s 1996 grant, yet the exclusions apply only to tickets sold at US points of sale, and the Brueckner and Singer analysis found carve-outs typically had no measurable fare effect. DOT has also said that carve-outs can inhibit the efficiencies of a metal-neutral venture, and it has not required them when partners proposed one.

    Immunity can also reshape who competes at all, as a study cited by Brueckner and Singer found that nonaligned carriers’ traffic between alliance hubs and other cities fell as alliances formed, which its authors read as foreclosure, and another found that immunity lowers partners’ costs, making them more formidable and potentially discouraging entry. The video counters that non-immunized partnerships, such as codeshares with Qatar Airways, Emirates, and Riyadh Air, deliver network integration without antitrust waivers.

    A federal appeals court recently signaled how much analysis a regulator must show before curtailing an immunized venture. On August 20, 2026, the Eleventh Circuit vacated DOT’s order ending the Delta and Aeromexico joint venture because the agency relied on conditions at a single airport instead of conducting the comprehensive country-pair and city-pair analysis it had always used before. Any future challenge to a transatlantic venture would therefore need route-level fare evidence of the kind the Justice Department economists assembled, and that evidence now looks dated, since the Justice Department paper uses data through 2010 and the Transportation Department study stops at 2016.

    Sources indicate that the next test is already forming, since on November 4, Lufthansa asked DOT to complete its review of a request to add ITA Airways to the United, Lufthansa, and Air Canada venture. A decision will show whether regulators weigh nonstop harm against connecting benefits when partners expand a venture rather than when they first form one.

    According to recent reports, the research points toward a narrower remedy than the all-or-nothing debate suggests, because harm concentrates in economy-class nonstop overlaps, business fares show little overlap effect, and connecting passengers gain from integration. Conditions that tie immunity to measurable capacity or slot commitments on specific overlapping routes, with published fare data to verify results, would test the claim that partners deliver benefits unaided competition would not. Until such data exist, both the cartel label and the efficiency defense will remain easier to assert than to prove.

    This Is American Airlines’ Oldest Aircraft Type Flying In 2026

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1488 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines touts its flightline as one of the newest in North America, yet dozens of quarter-century-old narrowbodies still fly daily itineraries at its busiest hubs.
    • Sources indicate that AA plans to retain the 48-aircraft A320 subfleet in service into next year.
    • On June 21, the 27-year-old N107US returned from a three-month retrofit as the testbed for an interior overhaul.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines touts its flightline as one of the newest in North America, yet dozens of quarter-century-old narrowbodies still fly daily itineraries at its busiest hubs. That largely comes down to the fact that AA acquired all 48 of its older Airbus A320-200 aircraft. Now averaging around 25.7 years old, according to ch-aviation fleet data, the planes arrived via previous mergers with two defunct carriers.

    Sources indicate that AA plans to retain the 48-aircraft A320 subfleet in service into next year. It even purchased one off lease last year instead of retiring the jets alongside its previous McDonnell Douglas MD-80, Boeing 757-200, and Airbus A330-200.

    On June 21, the 27-year-old N107US returned from a three-month retrofit as the testbed for an interior overhaul. On June 23, AA Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden revealed that the cabin refresh introduces updated premium seating, expanded overhead bins, and in-seat device power.

    It can be described as something like getting on a flying hand-me-down when you board an American A320 today. The earliest aircraft in that group began in Phoenix in 1990 when Edward Beauvais, the founder of America West Airlines, acquired aircraft abandoned by the insolvent Braniff Airlines. AA still operates all 26 of the single-aisle workhorses that America West eventually assembled.

    In 1996, US Airways took a desperate risk of its own. US Airways Chairman Stephen Wolf and President Rakesh Gangwal went on an Airbus 'shopping spree' to replace outdated Boeing and Douglas aircraft in an attempt to pull out of a tailspin. "When I came here, it was a very troubled firm. People had given up hope of US Airways ever being a force in the marketplace," Gangwal later recalled, according to Wharton Magazine.

    US Airways started flying its own batch of 22 A320-200s soon after, setting up an awkward snag for passengers and mechanics alike. America West Airlines took over US Airways before the combined group merged into AA in 2015. All that corporate matchmaking dumped two completely separate Airbus fleets onto the same AA schedule.

    Recent findings suggest that for everyday flyers, that merger left behind 48 mismatched A320s with an expensive quirk under the wings. Because America West and US Airways chose rival engine makers, AA must still stock separate spare parts and run different maintenance playbooks for two tiny subfleets. Those upkeep headaches persisted even as AA executives packed tighter seating rows and leaner amenities onto those aging cabins.

    Under the 2018 'Project Oasis,' American decided to pack tighter rows onto its A320s. AA opted not to install seatback displays, cut back on galleys, and thinned out seat cushions. Matters were even worse on the 737 and A321s, which saw screens removed and seat pitch reduced. The president of the flight attendants union, Lori Bassani, noted the following year, as Fox News reported:.

    "We find that the seats are not only getting smaller, but there's no padding on them anymore. It is a torture chamber for our customers and for us, that also fly on our own airlines.".

    Prior to the 2019 Boeing 737 MAX groundings, the pandemic, and chronic plant delays at Boeing and Airbus, AA had intended to retire the cramped A320s sooner. Instead of easing out of service, those older jets kept flying as many as eight short domestic hops a day on flights under two hours. All those daily takeoffs and landings age an airplane much faster than smooth, long-haul cruising.

    According to recent reports, keeping all 48 A320s flying through busy hubs in Phoenix, Charlotte, and Philadelphia helped AA keep schedules intact whenever new jet deliveries fell behind. Schedulers leaned on those midsize jets to fill routes too substantial for regional planes yet too small for larger airliners. Even so, running 1990s jets alongside modern single-aisle planes indicates clear limits in seat count, flying range, and fuel efficiency.

    According to recent reports, stepping aboard an aging American Airlines Airbus A320-200 can feel surprisingly roomy compared with American Airlines' newer Boeing narrowbodies. While the spec table shows the older Airbus trailing American's Boeing 737-800 and 737 MAX 8 on capacity, range, and fuel burn, the matchup narrows to a window or middle seat.

    Industry observers note that an A320-200 cabin measures seven inches (18 cm) wider than a 737 cabin, giving flyers in tight 3-3 rows more shoulder room and aisle space. American CEO Robert Isom often spotlights fleet renewal, saying that "over the past decade, we have invested heavily to modernize and simplify our fleet, which is the largest and youngest among US network carriers.".

    Even with a 14.7-year average fleet age beating Delta Air Lines and United Airlines, AA still flies A320-200s daily. They fly out of Dallas/Fort Worth, Phoenix, Charlotte, and Philadelphia on routes like Dallas/Fort Worth–San Antonio, Boston–Philadelphia, and Cabo San Lucas–Phoenix.

    Unrefurbished A320-200 cabins still show their age with worn trim and cramped overhead bins, though American Airlines is closing that gap. According to aeroLOPA, this year's updated A320-200 cabin layout expands first class to 16 seats alongside 134 Main Cabin seats and adds larger Airbus XL overhead storage. Those larger lockers cut down on gate-check scrambles while preserving the A320-200's wider cabin for passengers.

    It has been revealed that boeing's newer 737-800 and 737 MAX 8 jets do not automatically deliver a better onboard ride, either. According to View from the Wing, AA's dense 'Oasis' 737 retrofits stripped away seatback screens, packed in extra rows with less room even in first class, and shrank the lavatories. That era without seatback monitors will eventually end for both narrowbody families.

    AirlineGeeks reports that American doesn't strategy to install newly introduced seatback entertainment until 2028. For crews and operators, the A320-200 and 737 force clear trade-offs. Flight attendants get more aisle space on the A320-200 and avoid the tightest retrofitted 737 rear lavatories, while pilots trade Boeing's yoke for an Airbus sidestick and tray table on shorter daily runs.

    Unlike modern carbon fiber planes such as American Boeing 787-8s, the A320-200 still relies on aluminum for 70% to 80% of its structure. Under the wings, AA's two mismatched engine types also behave differently, burning fuel and wearing out parts on separate schedules. Even the A320's digital controls hit an unexpected snag last November, when Airbus linked an uncommanded midair pitch shift to cosmic activity scrambling onboard software.

    Airbus warned in an urgent global bulletin to airlines in November 2025 that "analysis of a recent event involving an A320 Family aircraft has revealed that intense solar radiation may corrupt data critical to the functioning of flight controls." AA's technicians worked overtime across Thanksgiving weekend to install two-hour software fixes across 209 A320 family narrowbodies.

    Industry observers note that those emergency patches cleared promptly once crews finished the holiday push. Still, keeping aging Airbus jets flying safely takes far more than quick code updates, as rising airframe repair bills and cabin upgrades push maintenance costs steadily higher.

    Recent findings suggest that keeping 1990s A320s flying is pushing American's repair bills steadily higher. Mainline maintenance and parts spending jumped 7.8% through the first nine months of this year after heavier airframe checks drove costs up last year. Worse, because American Airlines leases 36 of its 48 A320-200 aircraft, delivery delays force costly lease extensions.

    It has been revealed that that prompted American Airlines to add power outlets, larger bins, and four extra first class seats with privacy wings. That A320-200 cabin makeover leaves travelers and flight attendants with less room to move. First class row spacing tightens to 36 inches (91 cm) while standard economy squeezes down to 30 inches (76 cm), forcing cabin crews to serve more premium flyers from compact galleys with unchanged rear bathrooms.

    Even as American Airlines brings Starlink Wi-Fi across its mainline fleet starting early next year, these 48 retiring A320-200s will miss the 2028 seatback screen rollout. Federal airworthiness recalls are catching up with AA's aging A320s which compounds maintenance intensity even further. An August order for Aero Engines V2500 turbofan compressor blades caught the 26 former America West jets flying for AA in its net.

    Sources indicate that the directive comes alongside other recent recalls and proposals including work on evacuation slides, landing gear doors, and preemptive wing crack checks. Still, A320 family check pilots flew 42 transatlantic training runs last year to prepare line crews for American Airlines' A321-200XLR launch. Retiring all 48 A320-200 jets depends on hundreds of Airbus and Boeing replacements still working through factory backlogs.

    Although the Boeing 737 MAX 7 and larger MAX 10 cleared FAA certification in August and October, initial deliveries wait until next year. That timeline keeps American Airlines' oldest single-aisle jets flying toward 2030, bridging the gap until incoming 737 MAX, A321XLR, and future widebody aircraft reshape American Airlines' fleet.

    Sources indicate that sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    According to recent reports, saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care proposal if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

    Sources indicate that democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

    Industry observers note that sanders noted Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

    It has been revealed that his version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

    The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

    In a recent development, “If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders stated, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

    Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

    While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of Fresh York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

    Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”.

    Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

    In a recent development, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    Sources indicate that in addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

    To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”.

    Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee problems, he looks forward to finding common ground.

    ICAO Hosts Air Transport Conference, Elects Newly introduced Council Members

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Last week, ICAO Headquarters in Montréal hosted the Seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference, where Member States and industry stakeholders gathered to set global policy priorities on aviation economic regulation, infrastructure financing, resilience, consumer protection and sustainable growth.
    • In a recent development, over 1,500 delegates from 154 Member States and organizations attended the week-long event thirteen years after the Sixth Conference in 2013.
    • “Broad agreement was reached on the need for harmonized, risk-based, and proportionate economic regulation that facilitates the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, automation, sustainable aviation fuels, and advanced air mobility solutions,” ICAO said in a press release during the Conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last week, ICAO Headquarters in Montréal hosted the Seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference, where Member States and industry stakeholders gathered to set global policy priorities on aviation economic regulation, infrastructure financing, resilience, consumer protection and sustainable growth.

    In a recent development, over 1,500 delegates from 154 Member States and organizations attended the week-long event thirteen years after the Sixth Conference in 2013. They discussed high-level topics in commercial aviation: modernizing economic and legal frameworks, investing in infrastructure and skilled workforces, and ensuring that innovation keeps pace with rapidly changing technologies and global demands.

    “Broad agreement was reached on the need for harmonized, risk-based, and proportionate economic regulation that facilitates the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, automation, sustainable aviation fuels, and advanced air mobility solutions,” ICAO said in a press release during the Conference.

    Participants agreed on the value of frameworks that support innovation and investment for economic development. They stressed this especially for smaller landlocked States, which depend heavily on air connectivity for growth.

    It has been revealed that the Conference supported modernizing air navigation infrastructure in line with ICAO’s Global Air Navigation Initiative. It also supported liberalizing air services agreements without making liberalization conditional on infrastructure development, since upcoming air links fostered by more liberal agreements are seen as key to economic growth.

    However, all initiatives should be flexible enough to address local circumstances and should not burden developing States. ICAO’s statement continued: “The Conference also reaffirmed that international standards are key to building effective, market-enabling policies and avoiding fragmentation that could impede cross-border air services. Delegates pointed to ICAO’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) as a successful example of this approach.”.

    Participants were asked to express their views on the documentation proposing various initiatives with regards to consumer protection legislations that have become an integral part of the legal framework for all air operators.

    Industry observers note that at the Sixth Worldwide Air Transport Conference in March 2013, ICAO was asked to develop Core Principles on consumer protection. The final document, adopted by the ICAO Council in 2015, contains provisions on:.

    Industry observers note that the report for the Seventh Conference invites States to modernize their consumer-protection frameworks, keeping them evidence-based, proportionate, accessible and responsive to the changing realities of commercial air transport. It also notes legislation should establish clear responsibilities for carriers, intermediaries and other providers regarding information, complaints and disruption assistance.

    Industry observers note that ICAO is expected to review its Core Principles while preserving national and regional flexibility. It is also expected to assess whether existing policies adequately cover online intermediaries and other overlooked situations.

    Many Member States cautioned against the ICAO Air Passenger Handbook proposed by IATA, because producing and maintaining a single repository covering many different national laws would be too costly.

    The Conference asked ICAO to “examine the need for harmonized, risk-based guidance on the use of AI in aviation, including common terminology and meaningful human oversight.”.

    The rapid development of AI and its unknown effects on aviation operations is a topic Member States will need to monitor. ICAO will coordinate and facilitate international exchange, while States will oversee implementation to ensure that the technologies adopted are secure, interoperable and consistent with cybersecurity and data-protection objectives.

    ICAO will handle AI within its existing structure, as the proposal to create an ad hoc unit was not supported.

    During the final two days of the Conference, ICAO held an Extraordinary Session of its Assembly to elect the four additional Council members required by the entry into force of the 2013 protocol amending the Convention on International Civil Aviation. The Council is the Organization’s permanent governing body, accountable to the Assembly and responsible for setting priorities and implementing its directions. Its membership increased from 36 to 40, and there are no permanent seats.

    According to recent reports, six candidates competed for the four new seats: Ethiopia, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Oman, Thailand and Türkiye. In the vote on the final day, Kazakhstan and Thailand were not elected, and the other four States won seats.

    The Council now comprises Angola, Argentina, Australia, Belize, Brazil, Canada, China, Colombia, Cuba, Denmark, Ecuador, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Ethiopia, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Mali, Mexico, Morocco, Nigeria, Oman, Poland, Qatar, the Republic of Korea, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, Uganda, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the United States and Uruguay.

    The next elections will take place at the General Assembly in September 2028.

    The saga continues between the world's largest operator of the Boeing 737, Southwest Airlines, and the Piquette Family. Earlier this month, Jason Piquette and his family, including twins, had traveled with Southwest to Portland (PDX) in Oregon, and when they arrived, they noticed that their double stroller was badly damaged.

    Southwest initially denied that the airline had damaged the stroller, which turned a routine baggage policy complaint into an accusationwhere the carrier told USA Today that they had offered the Piquette family compensation, a claim that has been disputed by the family on TikTok.

    On November 7, the Piquette family had flown to Portland to visit family, and on arrival from their Southwest flight, identified that the stroller they had checked into the hold had been delivered with damage sustained, including bent and wobbly wheels, and a damage to the stroller frame.

    According to recent reports, piquette challenged the airline, but the airport personnel for Southwest initially denied liability and claimed the airline's limited release of liability policy, which suggests that strollers and car seats travel at the passenger's own risk. This left the Piquette family without a stroller for their visit to Oregon, leading Piquette to take to social media and repeatedly ask the airline for answers.

    Simple Flying reached out to Southwest for comment on the matter; however, an airline spokesperson could not immediately be reached.

    After Piquette's initial videos on social media were seen by millions, a Southwest executive contacted Piquette, who, according to the traveler, noted that the airline refused to reconsider the limited liability policy. The executive is claimed to have said, 'I'm the highest up person you're gonna get'. On the call, a $200 flight voucher was offered, with an expiry date as offered. Piquette outlined that this voucher would be 'useless', as he and his family had no intention of flying the airline again.

    Despite being several weeks after the initial incident, a recent report by USA Today has surfaced, following the Dallas-based airline confirming to the major news outlet that a $500 reimbursement for the stroller, in addition to the $200 flight voucher, was offered. This upset Piquette, which resulted in him posting another video asking for Southwest to explain why they "lied".

    Piquette has repeatedly called out to ask why Southwest misled USA Today, suggesting that the airline was trying to 'save face', after confirming that during his call with the airline executive, no $500 reimbursement was offered.

    According to the US Department of Transportation (DOT) ruling, all major carriers are liable for up to $4,700 for lost, damaged, or delayed domestic checked baggage. However, airlines often require passengers to sign or accept limited release waivers, which apply automatically under the Contract of Carriage that is agreed to when purchasing a ticket. This move exempts the airline from damage claims unless the item is lost completely.

    Piquette's use of social media has highlighted his ongoing frustration with Southwest, as the airline has continuously refused to replace or acknowledge the damage to the essential stroller. Through Piqeutte's videos, a number of people have offered donations, and even one viewer lent the family a stroller to borrow during their time in Oregon.

    Industry observers note that simple Flying asked Southwest Airlines whether they had any immediate prepares to review its limited release of liability policy following the event and following the widespread media attention this incident has created. Families traveling with young children on Southwest are entitled to an additional child item on top of the existing checked baggage allowance; this includes one stroller and one car seat/child restraint per child at no extra cost.

    Restored to Calder’s plan, the clouds are spinning again

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday.
    • The day after Alexander Calder presented his initiative for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.
    • Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The day after Alexander Calder presented his initiative for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

    Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

    “It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”.

    It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

    Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

    According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”.

    “It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he mentioned. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”.

    It has been revealed that it was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

    It has been revealed that “We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”.

    Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

    “We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he noted. “Nobody got how big this was until it revealed up on their doorstep.”.

    Sources indicate that quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

    “Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

    Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

    “This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have major pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most vital and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement remarked.

    The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

    “It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

    It has been revealed that in addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

    But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and remarked he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

    Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

    “Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

    According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

    “These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

    Industry observers note that younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

    “I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

    Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

    “I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he noted, gazing up at it.

    Industry News: Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May.
    • Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.
    • “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

    “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

    Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

    In a recent development, at issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”.

    The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

    It has been revealed that advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the glitch.

    Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they strategy to bring up a vote next year.

    In a recent development, senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

    Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

    The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

    “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

    “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump noted, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

    Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

    While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

    “Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most crucial stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”.

    The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

    The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the glitch.

    Industry observers note that “Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to upcoming national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

    News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused complications for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

    Recent findings suggest that while the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

    Recent findings suggest that this ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

    In a recent development, at Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:.

    The glitch is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:.

    Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”.

    Japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

    I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse!

    While it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

    While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a new restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

    Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

    Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

    Sources indicate that ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the issue here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Playbill, a site for all things theater-related, posted a job listing seeking “comedic singers and musical theater vocal talent” to record George Floyd: The Musical, a new project by the Busted Broadway group based in New Jersey that “exists to shake the snow globe and remind audiences that laughing at dark humor is not only allowed but necessary.” On its website, the group’s tagline for the show is “The $20 Bill That Changed the World!”.

    • Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    Playbill, a site for all things theater-related, posted a job listing seeking “comedic singers and musical theater vocal talent” to record George Floyd: The Musical, a new project by the Busted Broadway group based in New Jersey that “exists to shake the snow globe and remind audiences that laughing at dark humor is not only allowed but necessary.” On its website, the group’s tagline for the show is “The $20 Bill That Changed the World!”.

    Recent findings suggest that playbill has since released an apology claiming it “incorrectly approved” the job posting for its site, and is now reviewing its internal processes. “We know this listing has upset and offended many, and the fact that it made it onto our site has disappointed those who trust us as an outlet. For that, we are sorry, and are committed to regaining your trust,” the statement reads. In response to the post, some people have demanded that Playbill take more accountability by explaining exactly how such a thing was approved for the site, expose who is behind the musical (though that was already public), hire more minorities to prevent similar wrongdoing in the future, and concern apologies to the Floyd family and the black community. Others have more firmly called for barring the musical’s creative leader from the platform entirely.

    Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

  • Norwegian Luna stands out among Miami-based cruise ships for its refined design and more intimate, upscale atmosphere, despite being smaller than some competitors.
  • The ship offers spacious and modern cabins, including exclusive solo and suite options, and features a wide range of dining venues—though many come with extra charges.
  • Entertainment includes tribute shows and unique experiences, but venues can be crowded and the ship has fewer large attractions compared to larger ships in the market.
  • Top-deck space is divided between family-friendly attractions and exclusive, extra-fee areas, resulting in a bifurcated experience depending on willingness to pay for added privacy.

    OMCO Solar offers solar-powered tracker control system

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OMCO Solar now offers a version of its OMCO Star Tracker Control System powered entirely by solar energy, allowing tracker controls to operate without AC power at the site.
    • The system, first launched last year, is designed for OMCO Origin Factory-Direct Trackers.
    • Sources indicate that according to OMCO, the technology eliminates the need for AC power to tracker control components and an uninterruptible power supply.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OMCO Solar now offers a version of its OMCO Star Tracker Control System powered entirely by solar energy, allowing tracker controls to operate without AC power at the site.

    The system, first launched last year, is designed for OMCO Origin Factory-Direct Trackers. Its tracker controllers, array controllers and sensor bridges use all-weather battery packs charged by solar modules.

    Sources indicate that according to OMCO, the technology eliminates the need for AC power to tracker control components and an uninterruptible power supply. It also allows tracker controls to operate and protects modules against wind, snow and hail before AC power is available.

    Sources indicate that “Our industry has solved so many problems as we have grown – we’re now the leading source for new electric energy capacity in the US. This addition to the OMCO Star product line solves one more – how to protect modules if there’s no AC power to the site even for a short time. We’re excited to offer this solution to our existing customers and to new partners,” noted Matt Kesler, vice president of solar technology at OMCO Solar, in a statement.

    The OMCO Star system uses LoRa, or long-range, wireless technology with a communication range greater than 1 mile. According to OMCO, this reduces the number of network controllers required and allows direct communication with every tracker without relying on a mesh network.

    The company says LoRa is 100 times less susceptible to electromagnetic noise than Zigbee and better able to connect to distant trackers despite obstacles.

    Sources indicate that OMCO indicates its all-weather battery packs allow the solar-powered controls to operate reliably in cold climates. The system includes field-replaceable batteries, a phone app that eliminates the need for buttons on controllers and a remote monitoring and control portal.

    Industry observers note that the portal allows operators to move trackers for activities such as mowing, snow plowing and module cleaning. The system is developed, manufactured and supported by OMCO Solar in the United States.

    Industry observers note that “We are excited about bringing this innovation to the Utility Scale and DG tracker markets. Over the past few years, OMCO has expanded its capabilities beyond just being a US steel manufacturer to now being a true technology leader in our space. We look forward to supporting our customers/partners with the OMCO Star Tracker Control System, improving reliability, and reducing the labor and materials needed to build their projects,” remarked Eric Goodwin, vice president of business development at OMCO Solar.

    OMCO Solar will display the all-DC tracker control system at RE+ in Las Vegas, November 17–19, in the North Hall, booth N516.

    Fascinating Air Saint-Pierre Domestic Transatlantic Flight Returns In 2027

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027.
    • In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly.
    • It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle!

    In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP).

    What’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people.

    The territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight.

    According to recent reports, this was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting:.

    It has been revealed that the route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing.

    The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027, between June 21 and September 6, 2027.

    Recent findings suggest that the route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows:.

    Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PMSaint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM.

    The 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week.

    In a recent development, I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare.

    If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares.

    As you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin.

    Air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was launched in the first place, and is sticking around.

    While the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route.

    Anyone else love this Air Saint-Pierre flight as much as I do?

    According to recent reports, I took this flight a few months ago, just for kicks. It's a fun thing to have done, but the flight itself is a routine experience. Many of the passengers were groups of school children. I could not determine whether they were local kids headed to mainland France or vice versa. AFAIK I was the only passenger who was not a native French speaker. The cabin crew, while reasonably bilingual French/English, seemed more comfortable in English. Immigration and customs procedures were those of an international non-Schengen flight. St. Pierre itself is not exactly exciting, but I enjoyed two days there.

    Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., mentioned he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).
    • If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday revealed how poisonous the politics could become.
    • Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., mentioned he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday revealed how poisonous the politics could become.

    Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

    “I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”.

    Recent findings suggest that johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

    Recent findings suggest that "This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”.

    But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”.

    In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”.

    Sources indicate that johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

    There is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson remarked Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

    And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

    Sources indicate that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

    In a recent development, A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

    Senators on both sides of the aisle stated they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

    Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

    “I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability concern, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” remarked Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.
